#3579. All Gold Skulltula locations in Ocarina of Time

How to save the cursed family in Kakariko Village

Gold Skulltulas act as a collectible in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, but they're also needed to cure a cursed family in Kakariko Village.

The poor family have been turned into Skulltulas, and the only way to cleanse them of their curse is to hunt down the Gold Skulltulas scattered across Hyrule. However, that's easier said than done, as there are 100 of them in total, and they're extremely difficult to find.

Here's where to find every Gold Skulltula in Ocarina of Time remake, and the rewards for curing the family in Kakariko Village.

[Ed. note: This guide contains spoilers for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, so continue at your own risk! Feel free to follow along or bookmark this page and come back later.]

As you collect Gold Skulltula tokens, you can turn them in to the cursed family in Kakariko Village for rewards. Every 10 Gold Skulltulas you collect from 10 to 50 will lead to a reward, but then you won't receive anything until you turn in all 100 Gold Skulltulas. After you collect 20 Gold Skulltulas, make sure to get your reward, as the Echo Gem is extremely helpful for finding the rest of them.

Below, we've listed all the Gold Skulltula rewards, and how many you need to turn in to receive them.

This big wallet, made for grown-ups, is able to hold up to 500 rupees.

Equipping this gem will help you detect nearby Gold Skulltulas through a combination of light and sound.

This enormous wallet is able to hold up to 1,000 rupees.

Once placed on the ground, this wall-climbing bomb zooms off on its own before exploding after a certain distance.

Collect four Pieces of Heart to gain a heart.

Every time you talk to the Restored Rich Man, he'll give you a gold rupee.

There are 100 Gold Skulltula tokens in Ocarina of Time. We've listed where to find every Gold Skulltula separated by zone. In each section, the Gold Skulltulas are listed in chronological order.

If you're looking for a specific area, make sure to use the Ctrl + F shortcut and search for its name.

[Ed. note: If you're viewing this guide on a mobile device, you may have to swipe left and right to see all the information on the tables below.]

In this section, we'll cover the 16 Gold Skulltulas found in the following areas:

In the room with the compass, look along the southern wall to find this Gold Skulltula.

Right after you fall into the giant spider web in the main room and land in the water, turn around to find this Gold Skulltula crawling on the vines.

Immediately after you grab the Gold Skulltula above, head into the next room, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula crawling on metal bars by the water. Shoot it with your Fairy Slingshot, and jump at the token to collect it.

In the room in the top left corner of B1, you'll find a Gold Skulltula climbing on vines. Be careful of the Deku Baba and Skulltula along the way!

Head to the east side of Kokiri Shop and place a bug onto the pile of soft soil to force a Gold Skulltula to pop out.

Go to the west side of the Know-It-All Brother's House at night, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

From the Kokiri Forest entrance, take the path to the left, and then take another left. You'll find a pile of soft soil on your left. Place a bug on it, and a Gold Skulltula will pop out.

From the Kokiri Forest entrance, go right, left, right, left, and left. Put a bug onto the soft soil and a Gold Skulltula will come out.

Go behind the House of Twins, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula. Use your Hookshot to retrieve its token.

From the Kokiri Forest entrance, go right, left, right, left, and left to return to the Magic Bean you planted. Get onto it, and it'll take you to a Gold Skulltula.

Head into the Sacred Grove, and progress until you reach the square-shaped path. Follow the path to the east, and look at the wall to spot a Gold Skulltula. Use your Hookshot to retrieve its token.

In the first room of the Forest Temple, look up at the tree on your right and you'll see a Gold Skulltula on the vines. Climb up to the branch, and use your Hookshot to retrieve the token.

After you enter the main room on the first floor, head up the stairs to the north. Turn around to find this Gold Skulltula on the wall to the southeast.

After you drop into the hole at the end of the untwisted red hallway, go through the door, which will take you to a balcony. Follow the path to the left of the southern door, and you'll see a Gold Skulltula on the wall to the south.

After you defeat the Poe sisters, ride the elevator in the main room. Enter the southern room to see a Gold Skulltula on the wall, but there will be a Skulltula that will block your path.

Return to the Forest Temple after you learn the Scarecrow Song. If you pushed the stone cube at the end of the checkered room, you can head straight into the northeast room and climb onto the stone cube. If not, you need to make your way to the checkered room and follow the hallway to the right. Play the Scarecrow Song, and a scarecrow will appear on the balcony above you. Hookshot or Longshot to it, and there will be a Gold Skulltula on the ground.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the six Gold Skulltulas found in the following locations:

Roll into the tree just west of the river near the Kokiri Forest entrance, and a Gold Skulltula will fall out.

Roll into the tree on the east side of Talon and Malon's house at Lon Lon Ranch, and a Gold Skulltula will fall out.

Bombs, Boomerang (young Link), Hookshot (adult Link)

Break the circular rock in the ground in the southern trees in Hyrule Field. Defeat the Skulltula inside, and then hit the Gold Skulltula on the back wall with a Boomerang or Hookshot.

On the western side of Talon and Malon's house, you'll see a Gold Skulltula on the window. Use your Boomerang to collect it.

Night, Boomerang (Young Link), Hookshot (Adult Link)

Go into the stone tower in the southwest corner of Lon Lon Ranch. Look up, and you'll see a Gold Skulltula resting on some vines. Use your Boomerang or Hookshot to retrieve its token.

Break the circular rock as young Link, and drop into the hole. Defeat the Skullwalltula on the back wall and travel into the future. Return to the cave, and you'll find a box. Roll into it and a Gold Skulltula will pop out.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the three Gold Skulltulas found in the following areas:

After you enter Hyrule Castle Town, immediately turn right and go into the door ahead to enter the Guard Tower. At the end of the room, a box will periodically jump up and down. Roll into the box to break it, which will reveal a Gold Skulltula.

Before you climb up the vines in the garden outside of Hyrule Castle, turn to the right to see a lone tree. Roll into it, and a Gold Skulltula will drop onto the ground.

Young Link, Bombs, Boomerang, Song of Storms

Play the Song of Storms by the tree by Hyrule Castle's moat. Drop into the hole, and blow up the rock wall to your right. There will be a Skullwalltula and a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Hit it with your Boomerang to retrieve it.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the 16 Gold Skulltulas in the following areas:

Go behind the northwest house in Kakariko Village at nighttime, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

This Gold Skulltula is found on the ladder of the tall tower in Kakariko Village at night.

Roll into the tree at the center of Kakariko Village, and a Gold Skulltula will drop onto the ground.

Near the center of Kakariko Village, you'll find a house that is under construction. Come here at night to find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

This Gold Skulltula can be found just beside the door of the Skulltula House.

Head to the graveyard with a bug in a bottle. In the northwest corner, you'll find some soft soil. Let the bug out of the bottle onto the soft soil, and a Gold Skulltula will pop out.

Night, Boomerang (young Link), Hookshot (adult Link)

This Gold Skulltula is found behind Dampé's house. Use your Boomerang or Hookshot to retrieve it.

Hookshot onto the vines to the southeast of Impa's house (the southernmost house in Kakariko Village), and jump onto the roof. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall to the south. Hookshot it to retrieve it.

Use the Lenses of Truth to avoid any holes in the floor as you navigate your way into the eastern room. You'll enter a room with a Like Like, but there is also a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Use the Boomerang to retrieve it.

Use the Lenses of Truth to jump into the central room. Use a small key to open the east door, and use the Lenses of Truth to spot an invisible pathway. Walk across it, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula in the corner of the room.

Use the Lenses of Truth to jump into the central room. Use a small key to open the west door, and you'll find a Deku Baba and a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

After you cross the bridge of guillotines on B3 and defeat the Stalfos at the end, put on the Lenses of Truth and look to the east. Put on the Hover Boots, cross the gap, and go into the room. Use the Lenses of Truth to see a scythe trap. Avoid it, and go into the next room to find a Gold Skulltula.

Enter the southwestern room on B3, and put on the Lenses of Truth to see a block hidden inside the wall. Use it to stop the spike traps from crushing you, and then climb on top of them. Ride them up, and you'll see a Gold Skulltula in the northeast corner of the room.

After you Longshot in the hallway with the fans and Blade Traps, turn around to find a Gold Skulltula on the wall below you. Use your Longshot to retrieve its token.

After you ride the elevator down to B4, pull the stone cube out of the wall and climb onto the wooden platform. Look to the caged area, and play the Scarecrow Song. Longshot to the scarecrow, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

Adult Link, Bombs, Fire Arrow or Din's Fire, Lenses of Truth

After you get off the boat on B4, set fire to the spider web covering the door. Use the Lenses of Truth to make it through the invisible maze, and enter the west door. Throw a bomb into all three rotating skulls, and a Gold Skulltula will pop out of the last one.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the 18 Gold Skulltulas in the following areas:

Blow up the entrance to Dodongo Cavern using the bomb flower above. At the entrance, you'll find a mound of soft soil. Release a bug onto it, and a Gold Skulltula will jump out.

After you first make it to the second floor in Dodongo Cavern, you'll find this Gold Skulltula on a wall at the top of the stairs.

After you unlock the Bomb Bag and return to the second floor of the main room in Dodongo Cavern, turn to the right to find a rock wall. Blow it up with a bomb, and you'll enter a room with two Dodongos and a large rock. You'll find this Gold Skulltula on the back of the rock.

After you unlock the Bomb Bag, head back down to the first floor. Follow the path to the east, where you'll find a rock wall. Blow it up, and head inside to find a Gold Skulltula.

After you head through the Dodongo skull, follow the path to the northwestern corner of the area. Move the stone cubes to the rock wall, and blow it up. Defeat the Armos and baby Dodongos inside to find the Gold Skulltula.

Between Dodongo Cavern and Kakariko Village, you'll find a rock wall. Blow it up with a bomb, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula inside.

Head to the top floor of Goron City, and make your way to the west side. You'll find a room full of rocks that you can blow up with your bombs. Blow up two rocks on the right side of the room, and then start making your way to the center of the room. Then, blow up the rocks to the west until you reach the wall. There will be a hopping crate in the northwest corner. Roll into it and a Gold Skulltula will pop out.

Run into Death Mountain Crater, turn left, and quickly roll into the bouncing box to find a Gold Skulltula.

Head to the east side of the first floor of Dodongo Cavern, and you'll find a ledge on your left around halfway down the hallway. Play the Scarecrow Song to summon a scarecrow, and Hookshot to it. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

Go down one floor in Goron City, and walk around the ring to the other side. Look at the backside of the central rock, and you'll find the Gold Skulltula. Hit it with your Hookshot to retrieve it.

After you learn the Bolero of Fire outside the Fire Temple, travel back to the past to become young Link. Then, warp back to the Fire Temple, and put a bug onto the soft soil to the south.

After you enter the first eastern room in the Fire Temple, follow the floating platforms in the northeast. The last platform will launch upwards to the higher ledge. Jump over and play the Song of Time to move the cube. Climb onto it and head through the door to enter a room with Flying Tiles, a Like Like, and a Gold Skulltula.

After you reach the third floor, take the path to the north, and you'll find a rock wall. Destroy it, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

After you make it through the room with the moving fire wall on the third floor, push the cube out of the wall. Jump to the platform in front of you, and play the Scarecrow Song. Hookshot to it, and then Hookshot to the platform nearby. Go into the room, climb up the wall, and you'll find this Gold Skulltula at the top.

Using the information from the previous Gold Skulltula, use the Scarecrow Song to make it to the fifth floor. You'll find this Gold Skulltula on a wall to the northwest.

After you unlock the Megaton Hammer and destroy the tiered statue near the entrance, make your way to the room in the northeast. You'll find Flying Tiles, a Like Like, and a black rock. Destroy the black rock with the hammer, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

This Gold Skulltula is found behind a rock near the top of the Death Mountain Trail. Before you reach the netting to climb up to the crater, you'll find a rock on your right. Break it with the Megaton Hammer as an adult, and a Gold Skulltula will be behind it.

This Gold Skulltula is found behind a black rock on the way to Goron City. The rock is just next to the bomb flower used to blow up the entrance to Dodongo Cavern. Hit the rock with the Megaton Hammer to break it.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the 15 Gold Skulltulas in the following areas:

After you enter Zora River, you'll find the Magic Bean seller, and a pile of soft soil right next to them. Put a bug onto it and a Gold Skulltula will come out.

Head over to the ramps in front of the entrance to Zora Domain. Walk up the first ramp, and drop onto the ramp below you. Walk to the lowest point, and drop onto the land below you. You'll find a Gold Skulltula where the ramp meets the ground.

Roll into the lone tree in the southeast corner of Zora Fountain, and a Gold Skulltula will fall out.

After you make it past hallway of Shaboms with Princess Ruto, step onto the button in the pit. Swim over to the vines, climb up them, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula in the alcove.

Return to the main room on the first floor, and drop into the hole near the path to the north. You'll see a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Hit it with the Boomerang to retrieve the token.

After you defeat the parasitic monsters on the first floor, drop into the new hole in the main room. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the ceiling. Hit it with your Boomerang to retrieve the token.

In the southeast room of the second floor, you'll find a large pillar covered in vines. On the back of it, you'll find a Gold Skulltula. Hit it with a ranged item and climb up to retrieve your token.

Climb onto the ramp south of Lord Jabu-Jabu, and hit the Gold Skulltula on the southern wall with a Boomerang.

Get onto the large rock formation in the middle of the river and head southwest. There will be a Gold Skulltula on the southern wall.

After you pass through the archway on the eastern side of Zora River, look up toward the east wall. You'll find a Gold Skulltula just out of reach. Hop onto the little railing and use Hookshot to retrieve this token.

Go to Zora Domain, and look to the south of the frozen waterfall. You'll see a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Go up the stairs and around the corner to reach the waterfall. Then, turn to your left, and use Hookshot to retrieve the token.

After you enter the room with the rotating blades and crystals, look at the southwestern wall, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula. Hookshot it to retrieve it.

In the eastern room, break the ice stalagmites in front of the chest. Turn around, and you'll see a Gold Skulltula on the right wall. Hookshot it to retrieve it.

In the western room, slide your way over to the platform with the ice block and crystals. Look at the eastern wall, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula. Hookshot it to retrieve it.

Adult Link, Silver Gauntlet, Lenses of Truth, Longshot

Head to the southeast corner of Zora Fountain. You'll find a black and silver rock that you can pick up. Throw them out of the way, and equip the Lenses of Truth to see the Skulltulas hiding inside. Defeat them, and climb up the vines. Walk to the edge and turn around to see a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Use your Longshot to retrieve its token.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the 10 Gold Skulltulas in the following areas:

Swim to the southwest corner of Lake Hylia, where you'll find a small tunnel entrance. Crawl through and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

Put a bug onto the pile of soft soil beside the laboratory, and a Gold Skulltula will come out.

Walk onto the bridge beside the laboratory, and then look at the building. You'll see a Gold Skulltula on its southwest wall. Throw your Boomerang at it to retrieve it.

Go into the laboratory and jump into the water. Equip the Iron Boots and sink all the way to the bottom. Use your Hookshot to hit the wooden box, and a Gold Skulltula will pop out. Hit it with your Hookshot again to retrieve it.

After you enter the central pillar, Hookshot up to the higher floor. Play Zelda's Lullaby to raise the water level, and use the Iron Boots to dive into the hole underwater. Defeat the enemies, hit the diamond-shaped switch with your Hookshot, and swim into the hole in the ceiling. In this room, you'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

After you raise the water level to the second floor, put on your Iron Boots and enter the room to the east. Take off your Iron Boots, and float up to the surface to see a rock wall. Destroy it with a bomb, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula inside.

As you're going through the river full of whirlpools, there will be a Gold Skulltula on the northern wall. Equip your Iron Boots, sink to the bottom of the river, and hit it with the Longshot to retrieve it.

Lower the water level to the lowest level, and head into the central pillar. Raise the water level once, and use your Longshot to hit the target on the ceiling. There will be a Gold Skulltula in the northeast corner. Hit it with the Longshot to retrieve its token.

After you make it through the room with rolling boulders and collect the boss room key, exit back into the hallway. You'll see a waterfall on your right, but if you look through it, you'll see a Gold Skulltula. Hit it with your Longshot to retrieve it.

Make your way to the large tree at the center of Lake Hylia. Use your Longshot on the vines, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula on top of the tree.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

In this section, we'll cover the 15 Gold Skulltulas in the following areas:

Drop off the edge to the right of the second bridge, and quickly swim to shore. Follow the path to the left, and you'll find a pile of soft soil. Place a bug onto it, and a Gold Skulltila will pop out.

Instead of walking over the first bridge, go into the water and look under the bridge to find the Gold Skulltula. Stand on one of the rocks and hit it with your Boomerang.

Go behind the tent in Gerudo Valley at night, and use the Hookshot on the Gold Skulltula.

In the area with a bunch of black rocks, look at the rock archway to find a Gold Skulltula. Use your Hookshot to retrieve its token.

From the prison exit, jump east to the rooftop. Go up the ladder and drop down to the south. Then, go up the next ladder and head inside the building. Longshot to the target across from you, and follow the path outside. Turn to the right and the Gold Skulltula will be on the wall. Hit it with the Longshot to get its token.

Make your way to the large target at the northeast end of the Horse Archery range. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the back of it. Use your Longshot to retrieve its token.

As you're following the flags in Mirage Desert, you'll find a stone structure. Go under it and take the ladder down. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall.

Night, Longshot (adult Link), Boomerang (young Link)

Head to the northwest corner of Evil Desert Colossus, and you'll find this Gold Skulltula on the wall. Use your Longshot or Boomerang to retrieve its token.

Place a bug onto the soft soil on the left side of the Spirit Temple's entrance, and a Gold Skulltula will come out.

Plant a Magic Bean into the pile of soft soil next to the Spirit Temple's entrance as young Link. Then, ride the Magic Bean plant as adult Link, and it'll take you right over a Gold Skulltula.

After you collect the five crystals on the first floor as young Link, the wall will fall, creating a bridge. Walk onto it, and throw your Boomerang at the Gold Skulltula to collect it.

In the room with the giant statue, look to its right, and you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

Boomerang (young Link), Longshot (adult Link)

After you make it through the room with the Beamos, turn around and look above the door. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the wall. Use your Boomerang or Longshot to retrieve it.

In the room with the rolling boulders and crystals, you'll see five alcoves along the walls. In the northwesternmost alcove, you'll find a Gold Skulltula.

Longshot your way onto the statue's right hand. Play the Scarecrow Song, and Longshot over to it. You'll find a Gold Skulltula on the ground.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

There's one Gold Skulltula at Ganondorf's Castle.

Go to Ganondorf's Castle and walk past the broken arch to the east. On its east side, you'll find a Gold Skulltula. Use Hookshot to retrieve its token.

Table graphics: Johnny Yu/Polygon | Source images: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo via Polygon

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart and where to plant every Magic Bean.

#3578. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, And More (Nov. 6-8)

It's the first full weekend of November, the weather is finally turning truly chilly, and Halloweekend is in the rear-view mirror. Whether you went all-out on your costume last weekend or you elected to slap a nametag with a different moniker on your shirt and call it a day (which is my preferred way to celebrate Halloween if asked to do so), this weekend is perfect for staying in and curling up with a fresh series or movie. So, what's new on the big streamers?

Between Apple, Peacock, Hulu, and Netflix, there's a decent spate of new releases heading to streaming this weekend (and some of them even dropped earlier in the week). Whether you want to watch a gripping spy drama, a truly ridiculous legal drama, a breezy sports comedy, a crime thriller tinged with romance, or a quick-paced series featuring one of the best and weirdest pairings in TV history, I've got you covered.

Director Adam Carter Rehmeier, known for indie films like "Snack Shack" and "Dinner in America," teamed up with modern scream queen Samara Weaving and horror staple Kyle Gallner for this year's "Carolina Caroline" — which just hit Netflix, marking its first home on a major streaming service. Weaving, who also led "Ready or Not 2: Here I Come" and "Over Your Dead Body" recently (and who's joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe to play Emma Frost), stars as Caroline Daniels, a gas station attendant who falls in love with Gallner's con artist Oliver Anderson. As the two make their way to South Carolina from rural Texas, they end up committing robbery after robbery, leaving destruction in their wake.

Weaving's Caroline and Gallner's Oliver make for a great modern Bonnie and Clyde, and "Carolina Caroline" is a gripping, entertaining, and extraordinarily fun film that also features Jon Gries ("Napoleon Dynamite," "The White Lotus") and Kyra Sedgwick in supporting roles. If you want a crime drama packed with plenty of romance, "Carolina Caroline" on Netflix is your best bet.

Congratulations to all bad TV enjoyers: One of the worst shows ever made is back for Season 2! Ryan Murphy's gleefully ludicrous legal drama "All's Fair," which undoubtedly gives real lawyers raging headaches if they dare to tune in, stars Kim Kardashian as high-powered lawyer Allura Grant, who works alongside Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts), Emerald J. Greene-Ball (Niecy Nash-Betts), Dina Standish (Glenn Close), and Milan (Teyana Taylor) at a firm that handles divorces. Sarah Paulson, a regular Murphy collaborator, livens up proceedings as rival lawyer Carrington "Carr" Lane, who is unbelievably twisted and extremely fun, and Nash-Betts, Watts, and Close are all game to ham it up.

I don't think I'm blowing anyone's mind when I say Kim Kardashian is a generationally dreadful actor who should not even appear in commercials, let alone a scripted drama that could be dishy and fun if she wasn't swanning around with absolutely zero expression in every single scene. Still, if you dig wildly bad TV and just want to switch your brain off, check out "All's Fair." Besides, if nothing else, it has given us an incredible episode of its fellow Hulu series "The Kardashians" where Close, out of character, gets very drunk off martinis at Kris Jenner's house.

I love "30 Rock," I have immense respect for weird little guy and short king Daniel Radcliffe, and I've been riding for Bobby Moynihan since the first time I saw him perform as Drunk Uncle on "Saturday Night Live." Essentially, "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins" — which stars Tracy Morgan, was created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, is executive produced by Tina Fey, and stars Morgan and Radcliffe as the unlikeliest and best duo in recent TV memory — was made for me in a lab. My enduring affection for this show aside, I think it's sure to delight pretty much anybody, and when Season 1 premiered in January, it immediately became one of the best shows of 2026.

The premise? Morgan plays Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced NFL star who was banned from the New York Jets and all other professional teams in the league after being caught betting on his games. (Hilariously, he only bet on his own performance to inspire himself to play better.) Thus, Reggie tries to regain his tattered reputation alongside his best friend and former teammate Rusty (Moynihan), his ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), his young but extremely compatible fiancée Brina (Precious Joy), his son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), and Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin. With Arthur living in his palatial suburban New York mansion to make a documentary that will hopefully relaunch Reggie's career and get him into the NFL Hall of Fame, Reggie does his best to refurbish his image, and the results are extremely funny. "Reggie Dinkins" Season 2 dropped on NBC and Peacock on November 2, and if you're returning to this near-perfect series, welcome back. If you're new, go laugh your way through Season 1, then join us.

If you enjoyed Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw's delightful spy drama "Black Doves" when it dropped back on Netflix in 2024, you'll be pleased to hear the series — created by Joe Barton — released its second season on the streamer on November 5. Across six episodes, we pick up where the show left off with Helen Dawson (Knightley), a secret Black Doves operative who sells secrets to the highest bidder and also happens to be married to a Conservative MP for a major UK constituency and Secretary of State for Defense, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan). In the beginning of Season 1, Helen is shocked and saddened to learn that her lover, Jason Davies (Andre Koji), has died under suspicious circumstances ... and her secret identity may now be at risk.

Throughout that first season, Helen teams up with her old friend and hired assassin Sam Young (Whishaw), who's sent by the Doves to help protect her. In Season 2, after a shocking cliffhanger ending, we follow Helen and Sam as he desperately tries to keep her safe, even as she's targeted by nefarious forces throughout England. Knightley and Whishaw are fantastic together, and if you sort of forgot "Black Doves" was a thing since Season 1 premiered 2 years ago, I'm happy to tell you that it's back and still an extremely fun and enthralling watch.

Apple TV has some of the best comedy series on television hiding on its service (which seems to get overlooked in favor of ones like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video), and if you're a fan of "Ted Lasso" but haven't watched "Stick," you're really missing out. Owen Wilson leads this sports comedy created by Jason Keller and stars as Pryce Cahill, a former golf pro nicknamed "The Stick" who's stuck selling clubs and coaching at a country club after years of a career decline. At work one day, Pryce meets a gifted young golfer, Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager), who quit golfing after some personal issues got in the way of his game. Determined to make Santi the next golf star, Pryce ends up roping him into a cross-country tour to show off his talents alongside Santi's mother Elena (Mariana Treviño), Pryce's former caddy Mitts (Marc Maron), and a onetime bartender and current caddy Zero Duffy (Lili Kay), all of whom pile into an RV to make the trip.

"Stick" Season 2 adds great actors like Timothy Olyphant (as Pryce's former golf rival Clark Ross) as regulars and guest stars like recent Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn as Pryce's former coach, with Billy Zane also joining Season 2 in an as-yet-unknown capacity. The first two episodes of the sophomore season dropped on November 4, so catch up before it continues its run.

#3577. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3575. 5 Years Ago: Benedict Cumberbatch Starred In Netflix's Best Western Movie

Jane Campion's 2021 film "The Power of the Dog," released five years ago this month, was one of the best films of its year. It was widely praised by critics and by the Academy, despite earning a tiny handful of cash during its not-very-wide theatrical release. The film was nominated for an astonishing 12 Academy Awards, including Best Picture, making it the seventh Netflix film in four years to be nominated in the top category (other nominees included "Roma," "The Irishman," "Marriage Story," "Mank," "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and "Don't Look Up"). "The Power of the Dog" ultimately only won one Oscar, for Best Director.

The film takes place on a ranch in Montana in the mid-1920s, owned by brothers Phil and George Burbank (Benedict Cumberbatch and Jesse Plemons). Kirsten Dunst plays Rose, the proprietress of a local inn, who is raising her teenage son Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee) by herself. Early in the film, Phil admires that Rose's dining tables are decorated with paper flowers, but becomes a little grossed out when he learns that Peter was the one who constructed them. This little observation kicks off the movie's powerful themes about traditional masculinity, gender dynamics, and the place of queerness on the open frontier.

These four characters get swirled together when George marries Rose and Phil's cruel nature reveals itself. While the young Peter leaves to go to medical school, Rose finds herself under pressure — more from Phil than from George — to be a "woman of the house." Phil insists, for instance, that Rose play the piano at a fancy dinner party, something she can't bear to do. By the time Peter comes home for a break, Rose has begun to hit the bottle.

We soon learn that both Phil and the young Peter are likely queer. Peter is more openly so, as he becomes fascinated by a secret stash of magazines full of hunky dudes. Phil, meanwhile, is very fond of a scarf that once belonged to the now-dead Bronco Henry, his former mentor ... and possibly more. Eventually, Phil begins to take Peter under his wing. Later in the film, Phil tacitly admits that Bronco Henry once saved his life during a blizzard by holding their nude bodies together. It's all but stated outright that Phil and Bronco Henry were lovers. This is the 1920s in rural Montana, however, so these men don't seem to have the freedom, nor even the vocabulary, to express their queerness.

At home, meanwhile, Rose's life is falling apart. She's drinking more and more, and her relationship with Phil is fraught. Although Phil eventually warms to Peter, he seems to place all his self-hate onto Rose, mocking her and making her life as miserable as possible. Phil is blaming Rose, it seems, for forcing him to reckon with his attraction to men. This leads to a late-film twist about rope-making and anthrax that leaves the film on a very dark note indeed.

"The Power of the Dog" is a marvelous tragedy of pain, self-denial, and gender roles. Rose cannot be the "sweet little wife," and Phil masks his need to be gentle and "soft" by affecting a "grizzled" exterior. Cumberbatch is fantastic in the role of Phil, capturing both his character's cruelty and his hidden gentleness. The film's title comes from Psalms, 22:20: "Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs."

Jane Campion's filmography is full of bangers, going back to her early films like "Sweetie" and "An Angel at My Table," through "The Piano" and "Portrait of a Lady," and up to "Bright Star" and "The Power of the Dog." This has been her most recent film to date.

Critics loved this movie, which earned a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes based on 363 reviews. /Film wrote that Cumberbatch delivered a career-best performance. Meanwhile, The New York Times' Manohla Dargis loved the sweep of the film as well as its treatment of the Phil character, a man who, she observed, had been "playing" a cowboy for decades of his life. About the film's visuals, Dargis wrote:

"A bold visual stylist, Campion introduces this world and its people with sweep and precision, with soaring eagle-eye aerial shots and her characteristic attention to voluptuary detail (and with New Zealand doubling for an unspoiled Montana). She fluently sets the western milieu, with its swirling dust and thundering cattle, and catches the boisterous camaraderie of the ranch hands, the playfulness of their jostling with its easy, unselfconscious physicality and intimacy."

/Film's Joshua Meyer wrote a full explanation of the ending of "The Power of the Dog," realizing that it's a tale of emotional terrorism and that it may be freeing to wriggle out from under the masculine lifestyle Phil was trying to perpetuate. "The Power of the Dog" was based on the novel by Thomas Savage, and Campion, who also wrote the adaptation, changed the ending (we think for the better). In Campion's version, the themes are incredibly clear, very moving, and pointedly righteous.

#3574. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3573. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Are Moving Again

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly found a new home in the Cotswolds, less than three months after their return to the United Kingdom. But anyone who thinks they’ve bought a new home will be disappointed. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who had been staying at the residence of a wealthy entrepreneur friend since August 26, have reportedly left the main house on the property to move into another residence located within the same estate, according to Daily Mail journalist Richard Eden. “They were living in the main house,” a person close to the entrepreneur told the British newspaper. “They have now moved to a property on the estate.” The move reportedly took place before Harry and Meghan left for a vacation abroad with their children.

Since the couple returned to the United Kingdom, their search for a new home in Britain has been a hotly debated topic, especially in light of their disagreements with the royal family and security concerns. The mystery surrounding their residence has fueled speculation and various theories. Where would the Sussexes choose to settle? That was the question echoing everywhere on social media and in the press. For security reasons, the details of their living arrangements have always remained confidential.

As reported by the British media, the couple and their two children had been staying at a property owned by a wealthy friend, nestled in the Cotswolds countryside—an area Harry and Meghan already knew well. In 2018, the year of their wedding, they rented a prestigious farmhouse in the region for two years—a historic property with an estimated value of 4.12 million British pounds (about $5.5 million), part of the Great Tew Estate. The residence included a four-bedroom farmhouse, a barn converted into living quarters, and a separate cottage with two additional bedrooms. The property also featured extensive grounds and a heated patio. Over the years, the Cotswolds, in the English countryside, have become a retreat for numerous celebrities, including Jeremy Clarkson, David and Victoria Beckham, and Kate Moss. A few weeks ago the Duchess of Sussex was photographed at The Three Horseshoes, a quaint pub near Burford, in the company of Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi. In 2024, DeGeneres and de Rossi left the United States to move to the Cotswolds, where they live on a large estate surrounded by greenery.

The Sussexes’ housing history in the United Kingdom, however, has been quite eventful. Before leaving the United Kingdom, the couple lived at Frogmore Cottage in Windsor, a property made available to Harry and Meghan by Queen Elizabeth II. In 2023, however, the two royals left the residence. The decision came a few months after the publication of the duke’s memoir, Spare. To renovate Frogmore Cottage, approximately 2.4 million British pounds (about $3.2 million) went into transforming two existing buildings into a single-family home. The renovations were extensive: The ceiling beams and floor structures were replaced, the electrical system was redone, new gas and water lines were installed, and a soundproofing system costing approximately 50,000 British pounds (about $67,000) was reportedly put in place. Despite the significant spend, the Sussexes left the property for good after moving overseas.

Even before settling in Windsor, Harry and Meghan lived at Nottingham Cottage, within the Kensington Palace complex. It was a rather small residence that apparently hadn’t won Meghan over. In the Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, the duchess recalled with a touch of irony that the name Kensington Palace suggested something grand, while the reality was quite different: “Kensington Palace sounds very regal, of course it does. It says ‘palace’ in the name. But Nottingham Cottage was so small!” Harry added that the house had very low ceilings and was even slightly slanted.

The new home in the Cotswolds could therefore be a practical solution for the Sussexes, at least until they figure out their plans in the United Kingdom. Meghan’s professional commitments may also take her away from England again. The duchess is expected to move temporarily to Australia next year to participate in the filming of Junior MasterChef, the cooking show she is set to cohost. Prince Harry and their two children might join her during her stay in Australia, but there’s no confirmation of that yet.

The identity of the estate’s current owner remains a mystery. He is a friend of Prince Harry’s, with whom he shares a commitment to charities that support veterans and military personnel. Apparently, the businessman would be happy to continue hosting the prince, Meghan, and their children for a long time to come. Several theories have circulated regarding the benefactor’s identity, with some speculating that he is Ian Wace, a British financier with an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion and who has long been close to Harry. He owns the Rowler Estate, a vast estate in the Cotswolds. His private life has been marked by tragedy: In 1994 he lost his first wife, Joanna, and their two young children in a car accident in Hampshire.

However, being hosted by a wealthy friend is nothing new in the Sussexes’ lives. In 2020, when they decided to step back from their royal duties and move to the United States, the couple stayed at the Beverly Hills mansion of producer and media mogul Tyler Perry. It was a Tuscan-style residence with eight bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, located within the gated community of Beverly Ridge Estates.

A few months later, in August of that same year, Harry and Meghan purchased a mansion in Montecito, California, where they settled. Surrounded by greenery, the mansion is located in a residential area frequented by some of Hollywood’s most famous stars, including Oprah Winfrey, Ariana Grande, and Brad Pitt. It is a very luxurious home that, at the time of purchase, was dubbed the Sussexes’ new palace—one the couple seems to have no intention of selling, despite their return to the United Kingdom. According to reports, the maintenance staff had continued to care for the family’s chickens.

The couple is still holding on to the California property, purchased for around $14 million, which continues to serve as one of their family homes. The estate includes a wine cellar, a movie theater, a gym, a spa, a large swimming pool, a tennis court, a wood-fired oven, a barbecue, and more than 13 and a half bathrooms.

However, this is not the only residence owned by the Sussexes. Just several years ago, Harry and Meghan purchased a home on the Portuguese coast, near the one owned by Princess Eugenie—Harry’s cousin—and her husband, Jack Brooksbank. The property is located within the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club, an exclusive residential complex with about 300 ocean-view villas in Melides, south of Lisbon.

Meanwhile, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected in Brussels on November 10 for an event dedicated to protecting children from online risks and abuse. The heart of the initiative, organized by MEP Antonio López-Istúriz White as part of a parliamentary intergroup, will be the unveiling of The Lost Screen Memorial, a video installation created in memory of children who lost their lives after falling victim to online abuse and exploitation. The installation will consist of 50 large-scale portraits of the young victims. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola is also expected to attend the ceremony.

According to reports in the British media, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint speech on the issue—which has long been a focus of the couple’s advocacy—before participating in a discussion with international activists. Among the scheduled speakers is Sandra Spitaels, the Belgian mother of Glenn, who, in 2017, took his own life at age 15 after a nude photograph of him was circulated online.

These two developments involving the Duke and Duchess of Sussex come as Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle, is at the center of a horrific legal case. He is the subject of an investigation launched following a complaint filed by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., with the Philippine police and the FBI. The younger Thomas handed over to investigators a box containing several images and videos that allegedly depicted child sexual abuse, found among his father’s personal belongings in Cebu City, Philippines.

Another discovery reportedly took place in recent days at a storage unit that Thomas Markle allegedly rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico. The facility was reportedly inspected by local police as part of an investigative operation. Meghan’s 82-year-old father has reportedly been transferred in recent days to a facility in Florida that specializes in caring for people with dementia, according to The Sun.

His move to a care facility could now complicate the investigation, particularly the possibility of questioning Thomas Markle. His cognitive condition could make it more difficult to proceed with the investigation, especially given the protections afforded to residents of specialized facilities.

Meghan, who has had no contact with her father since 2018, has not commented on the latest developments. It had previously emerged that the duchess, who had been aware of the allegations against her father since 2018, wanted to speak out publicly. One of the agents from Royalty and Specialist Protection (RaSP)—the Scotland Yard unit responsible for the security of members of the royal family and other public figures—reportedly advised her not to speak out. The agent reportedly told her, “Leave it with us, we’ll investigate it.”

Thomas Markle was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges connected to the possession of child sexual abuse material. He has previously denied possession of such material.

#3572. 23 Years Later, Buddy The Elf's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote Ever

When "Elf" came out in 2003, it established itself as an immediate Christmas classic, and on the movie's 23rd anniversary, we want to celebrate a simple, effective line from this Will Ferrell comedy which is not only fun for the whole family, but which has stood the test of time.

Before we get to the line in question, though, let's go over the basics where "Elf" is concerned. Directed by Jon Favreau (the Marvel and Star Wars one, not the political guy) and written by David Berenbaum, who wrote the movie after an earlier project called "Christmas in New Jersey" failed to take flight, "Elf" stars Ferrell as Buddy the titular elf, a human who's raised at the North Pole by his adoptive elf dad, Papa Elf (Bob Newhart, who also narrates the film). When Buddy sets out to find his birth father on the magical, mystical island of Manhattan, he meets Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical and uptight publisher of children's books who isn't super interested in dealing with any large adult son, let alone one dressed like a Christmas elf who pours sugar on his spaghetti. Thankfully, Walter's wife and son, Emily and Michael (Mary Steenburgen and Daniel Tay), love Buddy, so he's accepted into the Hobbs household and ends up saving Christmas.

There are a lot of great "Elf" quotes — and we'll feature a bunch of them shortly — but the one I really want to center is one that expresses Buddy's worldview perfectly. So what is it?

While talking to his coworker and eventual girlfriend Jovie (Zooey Deschanel), Buddy, trying to get her to sing in public, tells her, "The best way to spread Christmas cheer is singing loud for all to hear." Not only is this just a nice, neat little rhyme, it's also the entire essence of the movie.

Sure, Buddy can be annoying, loud, and weird; a grown man in an elf costume is a concept that's great on screen and would be objectively terrifying in real life. (It adds to the cinematic hilarity and imagined real-life horror that Will Ferrell is well over six feet tall.) Still, Buddy's big heart and intense joy ends up making everyone believe in the magic of the holiday season — even Walter, who eventually accepts Buddy as his son and decides that he wants to spend more time with Emily and Michael in the process.

"Elf" is truly a movie about allowing yourself to indulge in joy and cheer, and this Buddy quote is basically the film's thesis. That's not the only quotable line from "Elf," though; there are so many others.

When we received word that Marvel wasn’t moving forward with its Blade reboot starring Mahershala Ali, I have to be honest with you - I wasn’t heartbroken.

Now, this has nothing to do with the actor. I love Mahershala Ali. He’s super talented, and even though Blade isn’t moving forward, he’s still gotten rave reviews for other projects. Truth be told, the two-time Oscar winner has a right to be crestfallen, but he’ll be fine. Somebody as talented as he is will always land on his feet.

Even so, the reason why I wasn’t upset is that we still have Blade - and his name is Wesley Snipes. I know Feige and crew wanted to revamp the character, but why bother when Snipes is still kicking? I’ll explain.

We're two years removed from Deadpool & Wolverine, but can I just say that I still get giddy at all of the cameos in that film, namely Gambit, played by Channing Tatum, and Blade, played by Wesley Snipes. Their involvement was so cool, and I can attest that the biggest pop the movie got when I saw it back in 2024 was when Snipes stepped out of the shadows as Blade.

That’s because people LOVE Blade, especially Snipes’ rendition of him. This just got me thinking, though, because in the Avengers: Doomsday trailer, we clearly see Tatum’s Gambit fighting with Simu Liu’s Shang-Chi. So, if Gambit can return from Deadpool & Wolverine, why can’t Blade?

Granted, I don’t know if Blade is actually in the movie. Anything is possible right now with Doomsday's cast, but even if he’s not, why can’t Snipes return? I mean, the Fox X-Men are returning, including the late Patrick Stewart (RIP, Professor X). So why can’t Fox’s Blade return in his own new movie? That’s right. I’m talking Blade freaking Four, people! Don’t you think the Daywalker is due for another film? Because come on…

Unlike a lot of people, I don’t hate Blade: Trinity. In fact, like I said a number of years ago: Blade: Trinity is The Godfather Part III of superhero movies, and that’s okay. What I meant by that was, it’s fine, but it will always be in the shadow of its two superior predecessors. Blade: Trinity is just super forgettable, no matter how you slice it.

Should Blade really go out like that? I personally don’t think so. In the third film, we got some new characters: Whistler’s daughter, played by Jessica Biel, and Hannibal King, played by Deadpool actor Ryan Reynolds. That said, I honestly think these characters could just be ignored if there were ever a fourth film.

In fact, I think it would be pretty cool if a fourth Blade movie had the character surviving the Void in Deadpool & Wolverine, just like Gambit. He’d be scarred, of course, but still on the move, and I think the film could conclude with a proper ending for the character. Come on. You know you want it.

I was actually inspired to write this after going to a Halloween party. A good friend of mine was talking about Blade as if the movies had just come out yesterday, and I could tell that others still love and appreciate the character just as much as I do.

Also, it’s a shame that Blade kind of fizzled out after Blade: Trinity, even though he pretty much jump-started Marvel movies back in 1998. I mean, without the success of Blade, we might not even have the MCU today.

So, let’s bring Wesley Snipes back into the MCU. Come on. You know you want him.

That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3568. One Of Daredevil's Most Important Characters Was Only Supposed To Appear Once

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you asked Marvel readers to name Daredevil's most important supporting character, many would answer Elektra Natchios, the sai-wielding ninja assassin and Matt Murdock's sometimes lover, sometimes foe. But she came fairly late into the publication of "Daredevil." Created by writer/artist Frank Miller, Elektra debuted in 1980's "Daredevil" #168. The issue details her past of falling in love with Matt in college. In the present, the two are reunited because Elektra's assassin job brings her into conflict with Daredevil.

Miller had been drawing "Daredevil" since issue #158. He asked "Daredevil" editor Dennis O'Neil for a chance to write the book, and he turned it around completely. Miller transformed "Daredevil" from one of Marvel's least popular comics into one of its best, as his hard-boiled writing and dynamic action made "Daredevil" feel unlike any other comic. (Miller soon did a similarly influential revamp of Batman, which is why Batman and Daredevil remain so similar.)

"Daredevil" #168 was Miller's first solo writing credit on the book. His cover (inked by Klaus Janson) depicts a lightning strike, a fitting image for what Miller would do for the comic. That lightning conceals Elektra in shadow, while Daredevil looks on in horror. "Once he loved her... now she is his most deadly enemy!" the cover declares. Between the cover's imagery and the story promised by that caption, how could you not pick up this comic?

But at the time, Miller didn't see Elektra as the key to overhauling "Daredevil." In a 1983 discussion with Comics Interview magazine, Miller explained, "I came onto ['Daredevil'] thinking I was doing a couple of fill-ins on the writing. I ended up taking over the series, [and] had a character who was only supposed to appear for an issue take over the series on me — Elektra."

Frank Miller named Elektra after the Greek myth of Electra, the daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra who killed her mother to avenge Clytemnestra's murder of Agamemnon. Elektra Natchios is also defined by the death of her father, a Greek ambassador murdered in a hostage situation during Matt and Elektra's college years romance.

"Daredevil" by Miller takes a lot from film noir, and an alluring but deadly woman from the hero's past is a noir hallmark. Miller had one particular noir story in mind: Will Eisner's crime comic strip "The Spirit," particularly a 1950 story that introduced Sand Saref, the Spirit's childhood girlfriend turned femme fatale. Elektra's backstory — in love with the hero, rejects the law after her father dies, becomes an international criminal — hits the same beats as Sand's. (Bringing this full circle, Miller directed a "Spirit" movie in 2008 featuring Eva Mendes as Sand Saref, but it received very bad reviews.)

In the 2003 documentary "The Men Without Fear: Creating Daredevil," Miller recalled that he had wanted to introduce a new type of superhero love interest with Elektra, i.e. one who jumps across rooftops with her man. "Why wouldn't [superheroes] be operatic in their romance the way they are in combat?" Miller asked.

Knowing Miller apparently thought he might get one chance to tell Elektra's story, it makes sense that "Daredevil" #168 tells a complete and tragic arc. Daredevil and Elektra clash over the same quarry, and Matt remembers his past with Elektra (a blatant retcon, one smoothed over by Matt's inner dialogue suggesting it's been too painful to think of Elektra since). The issue ends with Daredevil revealing he's Matt Murdock to Elektra, but they still live in different worlds now. He then vanishes into the night, leaving Elektra crying alone.

Frank Miller actually brought Elektra back in his very next issue, "Daredevil" #169, but that appearance writes her out. She enters Matt's apartment, sees he's involved with Heather Glenn, and leaves, once more heartbroken. As Miller settled in on "Daredevil," though, he brought Elektra back in issue #174 as a regular character.

From there, she fought alongside Daredevil against the evil ninja cult the Hand and was hired to kill her lover by Wilson Fisk, the Kingpin. Fisk's former assassin, Bullseye, didn't take kindly to being replaced, so he murders Elektra in the double-length "Daredevil" #181. Elektra's fate echoes previous deaths of Marvel Comics female leads (now called "fridging"), like Gwen Stacy in "Amazing Spider-Man" or Jean Grey in "X-Men."

Miller felt that Elektra had to die or else she'd become an "insipid character," and he managed to convince Marvel's reluctant then editor-in-chief, Jim Shooter. But in Miller's penultimate issue, "Daredevil" #190, Elektra is revived by the Hand — unbeknownst to Matt, who still believes Elektra lost to him.

Elektra's resurrection opened the door for her to return, like in Miller and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Elektra: Assassin" or Miller's "Elektra Lives Again." Miller later revised Matt and Elektra's past in the 1993 miniseries "Daredevil: Man Without Fear" (drawn by John Romita Jr.), retconning Elektra into a dangerous thrill-seeker from the start.

Nowadays, Elektra sits as a permanent fixture of Daredevil's world, played in live-action by Jennifer Garner and later Elodie Yung. The comic Elektra even became Daredevil herself during writer Chip Zdarsky's run on "Daredevil." That endurance is not what Miller had wanted, and he admitted Elektra slipping through his hands "stings like hell" in "Marvel Comics: The Untold Story." If there's one publisher that won't let a good character go, after all, it's Marvel Comics.

When I think about the challenges that may have come with making Wicker, the wicker itself and the sheer horniness of the film (which the reviews pointed out) come to mind first. This project on the 2026 movie schedule required Alexander Skarsgård to be covered in wicker the whole time, and he and Olivia Colman have some very intimate scenes throughout the film. It’d make sense if all that was tough to work through. However, when Skarsgård was asked if he thought it’d be difficult to play the Wicker Husband, his response about why it was surprised me.

While Olivia Colman has been open about filming sex scenes in Wicker and working with the intimacy coordinator to make them feel “easy,” Skarsgård opened up about a different challenge that came with this movie. During an interview with the NYT, he explained that playing such a pure character was "foreign" to him, and that was a hurdle he had to get over:

There was a purity there that felt foreign to me. [Laughs] I had come off a string of darker, morally corrupt characters, and there was something so pure and beautiful about this character. It was a bit, I won’t say scary, but playing the nice guy is slightly out of my wheelhouse. It’s easier to find something interesting in the darkness of a character.

Now, I don’t know about you, but the last movie I saw Alexander Skarsgård in was Pillion. Like Wicker, it’s a romance. However, that’s all they have in common, and that’s especially true when you compare Skarsgård’s characters. The beloved Wicker Husband is so kind, gentle, and open-hearted. Ray, the biker he plays in Pillion – which is a romance involving a BDSM relationship between Ray and Harry Melling’s Colin – is incredibly closed off, demanding, and cold. In short, Ray is anything but “pure and beautiful.”

Along with Pillion (which you can stream with an HBO Max subscription), Skarsgård’s most recent projects include the concert mockumentary The Moment, the sci-fi series Murderbot and the war movie Lee, to name a few. None of those are the fantastical romance Wicker is, so this new movie required the actor to tap into a different side of himself.

Plus, as he said, it’s not often we see him play a genuinely nice guy, and I wouldn’t say his career is defined by wholesome characters. So, I can see why this role in Wicker challenged him. While the Wicker Husband and Fisherwoman have a very R-rated sex life, they have a remarkably loving and, in many ways, wholesome relationship. And while it was a challenge for Skarsgård to play that out at first, he nailed it, and he said he loved the experience too.

Now, if you’d like to see Alexander Skarsgård play a significantly less dark character than he’s usually known for, you can catch Wicker in theaters now.

#3565. Vija Celmins, the Ultimate Artist’s Artist, Gets Honored by LACMA

On Wednesday, I walked down Crosby Street and stopped at an easy-to-miss building where, high above the cobblestoned street, is the studio of Vija Celmins, who’s been there for almost 50 years. It’s a classic gigantic SoHo artist loft, the kind you’ll be shocked to hear still exist—but they do. In the 1970s, the previous tenant put a Buddhist temple in the front room. Not finding anything particularly wrong with that, Celmins lived in the temple for a while.

“Then I finally thought, gee, maybe I could put a couch in here,” Celmins told me as I walked in.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s been decades since the galleries moved from SoHo to Chelsea and got replaced by boutiques. But among this warren of cast iron buildings, some of the artists who moved in during the pioneer days remain. Among them is Celmins, the masterful pop-landscapist who paints in infinite textures, taking on the universal with an obsessive tenacity. The 88-year-old is a living link to a long-gone generation, and someone always in the running when we talk about the best artists who are both still with us and who began their careers before the JFK assassination.

Approaching nonagenarian status, Celmins is still incredibly quick, with a generous, buoyant voice. She immediately hopped down the stairs of her old studio and took me over to the windows.

“I used to be able to see down the street before they built this ugly pink building—all the way to the bridge, because this was a parking lot,” she told me, referring to a building erected 21 years ago.

She walked past a print she made some years ago: a depiction of the ocean, her most famous subject, installed on the wall. She admired it in a refreshingly objective way.

“It’s so loose. Usually I tighten everything down,” she said. “I mean, it’s such a relief. I had forgotten that. And what did I do? I only made 10 of them, which is interesting, in ’16. I must have done this at… It looks like it’s a drypoint—doesn’t it look like drypoint? I mean, I did a fucking lot of oceans, as you know.”

Though not a household name, in certain circles, Celmins has attained near-mythic status. The very few people I told about this interview ahead of time were shocked she was having anyone over to her studios in Manhattan and Long Island. She works incredibly slowly, and thus has shown incredibly infrequently. This has started to change in the last few years. She had a retrospective at the Met Breuer in 2019, and in the last few years, a few shows of new work at her gallery, Matthew Marks—the blue-chip commercial concern that represents a disproportionate number of the greatest American artists.

Next year, Celmins will have a show at Dia Bridgehampton. Tomorrow, she’s the guest of honor at the LACMA Art+Film Gala, a big deal in American museumdom. It comes with a gigantic bash presided over by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow. The gala’s also honoring Denis Villeneuve, which Celmins is excited about. She’s seen the Dune movies and, like Villeneuve, is a big fan of the desert.

During my visit, she opened up a random drawer under a drawing table. There was stuff everywhere, decades of sketches and notes and Post-its. She has a constellation of postcards taped to the wall, with paintings as inspiration, ones that look nothing like Vija Celmins—Picasso, Balthus—along with photos of her heroes and her friends with pets. There’s Jasper Johns with his dog, Borges with his cat. She’s got framed artworks from friends who are mostly dead now, like a Ken Price drawing of some undulating cups—“You know Kenny Price?”—and a very kooky, absolutely amazing H.C. Westermann of a wolf with its heart throbbing in its chest, wandering through the desert. Westermann made it for her. She made Westermann a wolf drawing in return. She doesn’t know what happened to her wolf.

There are drawings of globes, sculptures of globes, her tablet paintings, more prints of the ocean, a paperweight from an insurance company in Kansas City—near where she grew up in Indiana after leaving Latvia—a wrapped-up canvas labeled “ED MOSES” on the side, and plenty of drawings of Saturn.

She moved into the SoHo place after two decades working in Venice Beach, California. While in LA, she honed and refined, and inarguably mastered, a painstakingly laborious practice of applying graphite to paper in slow, methodical marks, rendering the passage of time in hyperreal landscapes. She now mostly works in a studio on the eastern end of Long Island, where she's had a place for the last few decades. But it’s here at the SoHo studio, in the erstwhile cauldron of cutting-edge American art, where she loves to be.

“The studio out in the country is more like where I went back to painting, really,” she told me. “And here I did all these weird things.”

This wasn’t the first time we had met. A few weeks back, I was admiring the very cool Gary Hume show that Marks had up in his gallery on 24th Street when gallery director Jacqueline Tran tapped me on the shoulder and asked if I would like to meet Vija Celmins. Vija Celmins! At the public opening!

We chatted for a few moments. She seemed spry, fit, with an elastic mind. Then she invited me over for lunch—not in the city, but at her place on farmland out east. On an October morning I hopped on a Jitney, then an Uber to Celmins’s part of the hamlet, which is essentially rural, with small clapboard homes encircled by crop formations.

I arrived at the same time as my fellow visitors: Michael Govan, the director of LACMA, and his wife, the fashion executive Katherine Ross. Celmins welcomed us in and introduced us to her cat, Raymond, who immediately pounced on my cup of takeout coffee.

“Down, Raymond! He’s very friendly,” Celmins said. “He’s my son.”

Out here, in the two-room studio attached to her house, she’s been able to conjure a vision of landscape perhaps more potent than the breakthroughs she came to so many years ago. In her studio, she showed us how the raindrops on her window, as captured in her work-intensive flattened plane panorama, could take on epic qualities.

We sat down for lunch—quiche and soup from a local bakery—and Celmins started telling stories about California. She hadn’t lived there in a number of years, though the topography of the state is what willed her artwork into being. She drove out to the desert with James Turrell, with Doug Wheeler, and spent years—decades—arguing with Robert Irwin, who taught her at UCLA. Irwin called Celmins his “star student.” I’ve always liked this Bob Irwin quote about Celmins: “Vija has perfect taste. She doesn’t like anything.”

Govan told her about the museum, LACMA, and the new building that had finally been completed earlier this year after two decades of planning and fundraising. Celmins was quite curious about it all. She has a few plans for when she’s in town for the LACMA gala. She seemed intrigued about meeting her fellow honoree, director Villeneuve, and watched the Dune movies in preparation. (I heartily recommended she watch Sicario and Arrival as well.) She’s going to visit her old studio at 701 Venice Boulevard, which she hasn’t seen in decades.

“I was going to go out in the desert, but I’m not going to have time to do it,” she said. “I might have to make another trip. I really like the Death Valley desert because it’s so vast, so terrific. And they have airplanes zooming from the Air Force around really fast. I used to wave at them. They go really low, and they just go like, vvvvvrrroooooom! Right above, following the outline of the mountains.”

She’s also going to see Riko Mizuno, her Los Angeles art dealer, who is currently 94 years old. But most of her friends are gone.

“A lot of them have died, I mean, I didn’t have that many friends, but some died, and some are dying right now,” she said. “And then they moved away. Ed Moses, I knew pretty well. Billy Al Bengston. Well, Kenny Price, I loved Kenny.”

Then she mentioned Robert Therrien—“You know Bob Therrien?”—the late artist who has become quite famous for oversized sculptures that are astronomically popular on Instagram. A retrospective at The Broad this year became something of a sensation. I can’t imagine an artist more different than Celmins—but as it turns out, they had a deep mutual respect for each other.

“I met him once, and he was a very unusual person,” Celmins said. “He was really tall, and everything in his studio was like—he had a ceiling that was maybe like 25, 28 feet tall. And he had this little ladder that went up this side to this kitchen, which was this kitchen he remade from Chicago or someplace where his family used to live. I’ll show you one little thing. He gave me this.”

She got up from her chair and found the Therrian artwork on a shelf. It was a snout, bobbing up and down in a terrifying manner, attached to a curved metal rod. Just the inner part of the face of a canine, floating forever.

“It’s so disorienting. Where’s the rest of the dog?” I asked.
