#3551. 4 Years Later, Captain Pike's Most Inspiring Star Trek Quote Is Still the Best Sci-Fi Line of the Decade

His future holds tragedy, but his most powerful speech captures the hope and optimism that have defined Star Trek for decades

For most of Star Trek's existence, Christopher Pike was little more than a footnote in franchise history. He was the captain of the Enterprise before James T. Kirk, a character whose greatest claim to fame was appearing in a rejected television pilot. Then Anson Mount came along and changed everything.

Originally portrayed by Jeffrey Hunter in "The Cage," filmed in 1964, Pike eventually became a piece of Star Trek trivia after William Shatner's Kirk took command. But when Mount joined Star Trek: Discovery in 2019, he transformed Pike into one of the franchise's most compelling characters. His performance was so well received that Pike eventually got his own series, Star Trek: Strange New Worlds, in 2022.

Suddenly, a captain who had spent nearly six decades in Kirk's shadow was giving fans a reason to reconsider his place among Starfleet's greatest leaders. And in the very first episode of Strange New Worlds, Pike delivers what I consider the most inspiring line in science-fiction history: "Until our last moment, the future is what we make it."

It's a simple statement, but coming from a man who knows exactly what his future holds, it's also an extraordinary one.

Star Trek has never lacked inspirational leaders. Kirk practically invented the template for the charismatic starship captain, while Jean-Luc Picard could turn a routine conversation into a speech worthy of a standing ovation. Benjamin Sisko led the Federation through one of its darkest periods, and Kathryn Janeway spent seven years refusing to give up on getting her crew home.

Pike belongs in that company, even if his leadership style is a little different.

Mount gives Pike a warmth and approachability that distinguishes him from his predecessors. He's confident without being arrogant, compassionate without being naive, and comfortable enough with his authority that he doesn't need to remind everyone who's in charge. He's also surprisingly funny, whether he's trading remarks with his officers or inviting the crew into his quarters for one of his elaborate home-cooked meals. Apparently, commanding the Enterprise leaves plenty of time to perfect your culinary skills.

But Pike's greatest strength is his ability to recognize the potential in others. He trusts his officers, encourages them to challenge his thinking, and understands that leadership isn't simply about giving orders. It's about helping people become the best versions of themselves.

In the Strange New Worlds premiere, Pike and his crew arrive at Kiley 279, a planet whose inhabitants have developed technology capable of destroying their own civilization. Starfleet is indirectly responsible, as the planet's scientists observed a battle involving Federation ships and reverse-engineered the technology they witnessed.

With two opposing factions preparing for war, Pike faces a choice: follow Starfleet's regulations against interfering with developing civilizations or attempt to prevent a catastrophe his own people inadvertently helped create. Naturally, Pike chooses the latter.

He shows the planet's leaders Earth's history, explaining how humanity nearly destroyed itself through escalating conflicts that culminated in World War III. But rather than simply warning them about the consequences of war, Pike offers them hope.

"Until our last moment, the future is what we make it."

It's difficult to imagine a more fitting statement of Star Trek's philosophy. Since 1966, the franchise has presented a vision of humanity that refuses to accept our worst qualities as permanent limitations. Gene Roddenberry imagined a future in which people from different backgrounds could overcome their differences and explore the universe together.

Pike's speech embraces that same optimism. He doesn't promise that creating a better future will be easy. Instead, he reminds us that our choices determine what comes next. It's not about pretending our problems don't exist. It's about refusing to believe they're impossible to overcome.

What makes Pike's words particularly powerful is that he knows what's going to happen to him.

During Discovery's second season, Pike experiences a vision of his future in which he suffers catastrophic injuries while rescuing Starfleet cadets from a radiation accident. It's the same fate established decades earlier in "The Menagerie," but Strange New Worlds transforms that piece of franchise history into something much more meaningful.

When we meet Pike in the series premiere, he's struggling with that knowledge. Yet when he encounters a civilization on the brink of destruction, he delivers a message of hope despite knowing that his own future holds tragedy.

The season 1 finale, "A Quality of Mercy," reinforces that philosophy when Pike discovers the consequences of attempting to escape his fate. Changing the future leads to devastating consequences for Spock and the Federation, forcing Pike to confront the possibility that saving himself could come at an unacceptable cost to others.

Pike ultimately accepts the future he has seen, not because he's given up hope, but because he understands that his choices still matter.

Four years after the premiere of Strange New Worlds, Pike's words remain a reminder that hope isn't the same thing as certainty. We can't always control what happens to us, but we can control how we respond to the challenges we face.

Christopher Pike may have spent decades standing in the shadow of James T. Kirk, but Anson Mount has given him a legacy entirely his own. And with one extraordinary line, he's reminded us why Star Trek's vision of the future remains worth believing in.

#3550. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Spain.

#3548. Thunderbolts Storyboards Reveal A Major Marvel Character Was Cut From The Team

Marvel Studios' "Thunderbolts*" assembled the most motley crew of heroes in the Marvel Universe yet, and turned that collection of ex-assassins and criminals into the New Avengers. The Thunderbolts/New Avengers stand out mostly due to their lack of flashy superpowers, aside from Ghost's (Hannah John-Kamen) intangibility and Bob/Sentry's (Lewis Pullman) shadow-controlling alter ego, the Void. The rest are merely highly trained humans, some with a boost from knockoff super-soldier serums.

But a leaked storyboard frame, credited to artist Anthony Winn, show a much stranger character was considered to appear in "Thunderbolts*" — The Man-Thing, aka Dr. Ted Sallis. (See the storyboards of Man-Thing in "Thunderbolts*" below.)

A mix of science and magic turned Ted into a giant being made of plant and swamp matter, the Man-Thing. Created in 1971 by Stan Lee, Roy Thomas, and Gerry Conway, Man-Thing has been a member of the Thunderbolts in the comics. Including him in the movie would be drawing on that history.

"Thunderbolts*" director Jake Schreier previously said, in an interview with SFX Magazine, that he had wanted Man-Thing to appear in the movie. But Marvel had other plans for the character, and "it all worked out for the best." Those plans were the 2022 Disney+ special "Werewolf by Night," where titular werewolf Jack Russell (Gael García Bernal) saves Man-Thing from being hunted by the monster hunters of Bloodstone Manor. Personally, I'd think "Werewolf By Night" setting up Man-Thing's existence in the MCU would've made it easier for "Thunderbolts*" to include him, but apparently that was not the case.

It was rumored that Marvel Studios was considering a "Thunderbolts" movie for several years before "Thunderbolts*" actually arrived in theaters come 2025. Rumors from 2019 suggested a completely different team line-up was in consideration: Ghost, Zemo (Daniel Brühl) from "Captain America: Civil War," Justin Hammer (Sam Rockwell) from "Iron Man 2," and General Thaddeus Ross (the late William Hurt), Emil Blonsky/Abomination (Tim Roth), and Samuel Sterns/The Leader (Tim Blake Nelson) from "The Incredible Hulk."

Ghost is the only overlap between this lineup and the final movie's. Instead, a mostly-reformed Abomination guest-starred in Disney+ "She-Hulk" while Ross (recast with Harrison Ford in the role) and the Leader were key villains in "Captain America: Brave New World." Zemo returned in Disney+ series "The Falcon and the Winter Soldier," which introduced eventual Thunderbolts member John Walker (Wyatt Russell). Zemo (who, in the comics, founded the Thunderbolts) was planned to appear in a "Thunderbolts*" post-credits scene, but the idea was scrapped.

The final cast of "Thunderbolts*" pulled mostly from 2021's "Black Widow," and could've gone even further. "Black Widow" villain Taskmaster (Olga Kurylenko) shows up at the Thunderbolts' first meeting but is killed by Ghost. She was meant to have a larger role originally, but that wound up on the cutting room floor.

While he didn't make it into "Thunderbolts*" and hasn't been seen since "Werewolf By Night," will Man-Thing return to the MCU? In a recent episode of "VisionQuest," the assassin Paladin (Todd Stashwick) mentions tangling with a werewolf who is a nice guy during the daytime. That's almost certainly Jack Russell, so the MCU hasn't completely forgotten about "Werewolf By Night."

Since Jodie Sweetin and Andrea Barber launched their Full House rewatch podcast, How Rude, Tanneritos!, plenty of BTS sitcom tea has been spilled. From the fact that producers had a preferred Olsen twin to work with to the anger on set when Candace Cameron Bure cut her hair without warning, there's been so much to learn about the TGIF show. And, on the latest podcast episode, it was revealed that one actor had “too big a pack” to be wearing biker shorts for a scene with Kimmy Gibbler, and this sounds so cringey.

In the season 7 episode of “Love on the Rocks,” DJ Tanner debates whether or not to break up with her boyfriend, Steve Hale. When she goes mountain climbing with Kimmy and her boyfriend, Keanu, she gains a new perspective on her life and relationship. While discussing the episode, in a recent episode of How Rude, Tanneritos!, Kimmy actress Andrea Barber exposed a rather revealing detail about her on-screen boyfriend that cropped up amid filming:

This poor actor, Keanu. So originally, he wasn’t wearing his jacket and it was just his shirt and his biker shorts. But, the bike shorts were a little tight. And a little too revealing.

Yes, poor actor! When you rewatch the episode, the biker shorts Keanu was wearing really did look tight, almost like spandex. And for a family-friendly show, it makes sense to cover that up. Like Sweetin humorously said, that’s just too much information for families at home to see.

It’s common for wardrobe changes to happen when an actor on a family-friendly sitcom is showing a little growth down there. That happened to Jaleel White when he was asked to hide his bulge in Family Matters. In the case of Brian Evans, who played Keanu, Barber explained that the wardrobe department had other ideas to hide that area:

They got a note. Costumes got a note from Video Village. And so, they had to quickly find this jacket. A long jacket to cover.

Well, I’ve got to say, the long jacket worked. You can’t see anything. Hey, you do what you have to do to keep the Full House episode G-rated.

Anyone curious as to how Brian Evans felt about the embarrassing wardrobe change should know he told EW that he “didn’t know what was happening.” Not only that, but he also revealed the priceless reaction his mother had when one of the crew members told him he had “too big of a pack" for a teenager on this show”:

I remember seeing my mother’s face sitting at the studio audience just beet red, laughing.

This certainly isn't the kind of moment I would've expected to hear regarding the long-binge-watchable show, but it's also a funny piece of information. Thank goodness the costume department of the ABC sitcom was right on top of it. Otherwise, I could imagine the producers receiving some not-so-flattering letters from parents.

It’ll be hard not to think about this little (or not-so-little) tidbit of information when watching this Full House episode moving forward. Still, the detail shouldn't be too distracting for audiences given how the jacket comes into play. Fans can watch “Love on the Rocks” and more episodes of the show by streaming them with either a Hulu subscription or a Disney+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3545. Why Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Thinks Sci-Fi Has 'Grown Up' Recently [Exclusive]

In an interview with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, Andy Weir, the author of the hit novels "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary," recognized that the world has never been more accepting of sci-fi. What was once relegated to the realm of "nerds" and outsiders several generations ago is now embraced by everyone. And that, Weir noted, has allowed artists to tell more serious and dramatic sci-fi stories. When a mass audience takes it seriously, the genre, consequently, grows up.

And Weir has been doing his part to raise the genre's profile. The films based on his novels — Ridley Scott's "The Martian," and Phil Lord and Christopher Miller's "Project Hail Mary," to call them out by name — are known for their scientific rigor (especially "The Martian"). And although possessed of fantastical sci-fi conceits, both movies pay a lot of attention to science, research, and the power of human intelligence. These are movies for grown-ups that don't soft-pedal or water down the details of astronomy, physics, language, or botany. As such, these films come across as being comparatively "adult."

Weir also credited this in part to the various superhero films that've come out in the 21st Century. Many of those movies have sci-fi elements, and even a piece of Marvel fantasy fluff can bring more grown-up credibility to the genre. As Weir put it, "The superhero movie phenomenon helped bring more science fiction elements into the mainstream."

To be sure, artificial intelligence, parallel universes, and time travel frequently show up in superhero stories, and the genre's popularity has made a lot of those strange scientific theories a regular part of mainstream thinking. Yes, in that sense, even the box office smash-hit that was "Iron Man" helped the sci-fi genre grow up.

The recent boom of high-quality sci-fi television also came up during this discussion with Andy Weir. Just turn on Apple TV alone, and you'll find the cream of the crop in terms of modern sci-fi TV, be it "Severance," "Pluribus," "Foundation," or "Silo." Commenting on this, Weir noted:

"I think [the genre has] grown up a bit. So, it used to be science fiction was the bailiwick of just nerds. In the '80s, there were a few sci-fi shows. There was 'Star Trek: Next Generation' toward the end of the '80s. Then there was things like 'Quantum Leap,' and stuff like that. But other than that, the sci-fi shows that did exist were kind of cheesy. You got 'Battlestar Galactica' [...] It wasn't big mainstream entertainment."

Some "Battlestar Galactica" and "Quantum Leap" fans might bristle at these comments, but Weir is right on one point: sci-fi shows certainly seem more common nowadays. That, he argued, along with superhero movies and people now having access to more high-tech items, have further expanded their tolerance and devotion to the genre. As he put it:

[N]ow we've had a whole generation of people grow up in the computer age [...] [P]eople are a lot more socially accepting of science fiction as a legitimate setting [...] I love that there are serious, very well written, innovative and unique science fiction shows out there now."

Basically, sci-fi becomes real, essentially, sci-fi movies and TV shows become more normalized. And especially with all manner of sci-fi films having recently earned billions of dollars at the box office, it appears audiences, in general, are willing to give the genre more consideration, allowing sci-fi storytellers to take bigger risks in the process.

There’s a lot of love about Season 1 of Prime Video’s popular hockey romance Off Campus. The book-to-screen adaptation has incredible chemistry, love triangles, shirtless hockey guys, and even a live performance from indie pop-rock star Remi Wolf. I’ve been spamming her music ever since the show came out, including her new album Mud. Her raspy belt is incredibly unique, and I only just found out that it actually got her pretty far on American Idol.

I’ve actually been a fan of Remi Wolf for a few years now, so I was pleasantly surprised when I started watching Off Campus, and she popped up as herself on stage in Season 1, Episode 1, which is available to stream with an Amazon Prime subscription. However, I had no idea this wasn’t her first TV appearance. Wolf was actually first introduced to audiences on Season 13 of American Idol, and recently reminisced with People about her experience on the iconic singing competition:

I got pretty decently far, and it was a cool experience to see how the entertainment industry works because I had no experience whatsoever in that world.

Wolf, who at the time was 17 years old, made it decently far in the competition after auditioning “on a whim.” She wowed judges Harry Connick Jr., Jennifer Lopez, and Keith Urban to make it to Hollywood Week before getting cut from the competition. However, the “Bottle” singer said she was grateful her time on Idol ended there:

I was such a baby, and I’m so glad that I was able to carve my own path as a baby growing into an adult rather than having that early influence on me by executives and stuff. I feel like my frontal cortex was not developed enough to handle it.

One thing I love about Remi Wolf’s music is that it’s her own unique sound, and I love that she has built her career off living completely true to herself, and that Island Records, the label she is signed to, has allowed and encouraged her to do that. I have to wonder if teenage Remi Wolf in 2014 could have predicted that her run on Idol, and eventual exit, would have led to a cameo on one of Prime Video’s most acclaimed shows of 2026.

Wolf first gained fame from her hit single “Photo I.D.” in 2021, and has since released three studio albums. Her performance in Off Campus features some of her biggest songs off her second studio album Big Ideas, including "Soup", "Toro", and "Alone In Miami."

Her latest album Mud was released on October 9 of this year, with the 30-year-old describing the project on her Instagram as “my favorite, my healer, my family, my precious, my blood, sweat, and tears.” It’s clearly her most vulnerable project to date, prompted by her decision a year and a half ago to become sober.

I would love to see Remi Wolf return to Off Campus in Season 2, which has officially been confirmed to drop on Prime April 28, 2027. The “Sexy Villain” singer said on the Zach Sang Show that she would be down to return, but that she has no idea where they would work her into the story, and I have to agree. However, I would love to hear some of her new songs off Mud included in the soundtrack when Season 2 premieres.

#3543. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3542. 8 Near-Perfect BioWare Games That Aged Like Fine Wine

Even the sonic RPG (yes, there was a Sonic RPG)

A pack of wolves can end a Baldur’s Gate 1 playthrough a mere five minutes after the tutorial ends. A squadmate you didn’t bother checking in on in Mass Effect 2 can die permanently during a mission you don’t get to redo. And a Sonic RPG on the Nintendo DS can end its story with the good guys saving the universe…then coming home to find someone named Eggman conquered Earth while they were gone. Most people know BioWare as the Mass Effect studio, which is incredible on its own — but that undersells the vast range that built the studio’s reputation in the first place.

Party-based dungeon crawling, approval systems other RPGs are still copying, martial arts combat, even one of gaming’s most infamous flops hiding a superb flight model: All of this and more is in BioWare’s back catalog.

Not everything BioWare made held up fabulously. Dragon Age 2’s rushed development cycle is still a go-to example of what happens when a good studio doesn’t get the time it needs. But that’s not a knock against BioWare. The studio’s less-stellar titles provide contrast that make BioWare’s lineup of all-time bangers look as good as they do. These following eight games worked well and changed the gaming industry — not to mention entire generations of gamers — forever. Whether you’re more into CRPGs, space operas, or Sonic, each of these are worth your time today. You’ll still be thinking about years after the credits roll.

Why it still holds up: Skip a loyalty mission, and that squadmate can die for good in the finale.

Ignore a squadmate’s personal quest, and you’ll feel it later. Not through a stat penalty, but through who’s alive at endgame…no pressure. In Mass Effect 2, Commander Shepard spends the entire game recruiting a team of specialists for a mission against the Collectors, a mission the game makes clear most of them aren't expected to survive. These include Mordin the salarian scientist with a moral debt to pay, Legion the geth who’s just trying to understand their own kind, and Thane the dying assassin looking for a moment’s peace. Every hour spent earning their loyalty pays off (or doesn’t) during the game’s final assault on the Collector base. Nobody’s safety is guaranteed; the game is not about to be merciful. Skip the wrong conversation, make the wrong call under pressure, and that character just doesn’t make it — no reload prompt, no do-over, just a permanent gap in your crew for the rest of the trilogy.

Why it still holds up: Companions approve or despise your choices in real time, and it’s still one of the sharpest systems in the genre.

Six different opening chapters — human noble, elf mage, dwarf commoner, and more — funnel into the same fight against the world-ending threat of the Blight. Pick a different one, and you’ll get an entirely different window into the world of Dragon Age: Origins, along with very different relationships with your companions. Your party members react to you, your background, your dialogue, and your choices constantly, not just at scripted checkpoints, which means they start to feel like real people. Morrigan approves of ruthlessness! Alistair absolutely does not! Push too hard in the wrong direction and your companions will leave (or worse). We’ll keep spoilers minimal, but this game has an ending involving a deal with a witch that could save your life — provided you’re willing to go along with one of the weirdest rituals of all time — that people are still talking about years after the game’s release. It’s still one of the most unsettling good-outcome, terrible-cost choices the RPG genre has ever produced.

Why it still holds up: Its alignment system tracks what you do, not what you say, and few RPGs have matched that honesty since.

At the midpoint of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, a routine memory-recovery quest turns into one of the most talked-about twists in RPG history. It works specifically because the game’s alignment system tracks what the player actually does across the whole campaign, not just what gets clicked in a single dialogue choice…so your fall to the dark side (or your fight to stay good) feels very, very earned and definitely not assigned. It’s a twist that other RPGs still get compared to today.

Why it still holds up: Real-time-with-pause tactics precise enough (and hard enough to learn) that a wolf pack can still wipe your party.

Long before Baldur’s Gate 3, and even before BioWare’s incredible Baldur’s Gate 2, there was a party of adventurers leaving the town of Candlekeep on foot and getting torn apart by a wolf pack within the first hour. BioWare built the game’s real-time-with-pause combat directly on AD&D 2nd Edition rules — a finicky and fiendish tabletop ruleset, thanks THAC0 — and refused to soften them for a new audience. It’s the game that proved a party-based RPG could run on a PC with real tactical stakes instead of just menus and dice rolls behind the curtain…and the game’s Infinity Engine became the backbone BioWare kept building on for years afterward.

Why it still holds up: You can swap fighting styles mid-combo…in case you feel the moment calls less for punching and more turning into a demon.

Set in a mythic version of ancient China, Jade Empire lets players swap fighting styles mid-combo without breaking stride — bare-knuckle brawling one second, elemental magic the next, a full spirit transformation into a towering demon the moment after that. The morality system, split between the disciplined Way of the Open Palm and the ruthless Way of the Closed Fist, judged actions rather than dialogue-wheel intentions, years before that became a genre standard. Jade Empire never got the sequel it was clearly building toward, but the combat system alone still feels ahead of where most RPGs’ approach to encounters eventually landed.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Why it still holds up: A hunger mechanic ties morality straight into survival, not just dialogue choices.

Built on BioWare’s Neverwinter Nights license and developed by Obsidian, Mask of the Betrayer is routinely called out as one of the best stories to ever come out of that partnership. Unfortunately, almost nobody played it at the time. But you should absolutely play it today, and here’s why: The premise alone is a gut punch. The player character wakes up cursed with a hunger that can only be satisfied by consuming other souls, turning basic survival into a constant moral trade-off instead of a stat bar to manage. Companions like the spirit-bound bear Okku and the exiled priestess Safiya carry entire philosophical arguments about faith and godhood on their shoulders. Neverwinter Nights 2 is an incredible base game, but the expansion still gets talked about because so few people played it nearly 20 years ago. Finding it feels like coming across buried treasure.

Why it still holds up: Yes, BioWare made a Sonic RPG. Yes, it was actually good.

In the middle of developing Mass Effect and Dragon Age, BioWare made a turn-based RPG starring Sonic the Hedgehog for the Nintendo DS…written in part by future Dragon Age lead writer Mike Laidlaw. Combat runs on the DS touchscreen, with rhythm-timed stylus taps replacing simple button mashing. The story leans harder into actual plot than anyone could expect from what could easily be dismissed as a spinoff cash-grab in lesser hands. Midway through, the Nocturnus Clan's own leader betrays his second-in-command by throwing her off a flying island mid-scheme, and the resulting crash sends Angel Island — yes, the actual floating island from the mainline games — plummeting straight into a city.

While it’s not quite a lost masterpiece, it is a competent RPG that just so happened to star Sonic…made by a studio that, it would seem, could not resist trying to mesh those two concepts. It would also seem that nobody involved phoned this one in.

Why it still holds up: Flight controls good enough to free-fall from orbit into an underwater cave with zero loading screens.

Anthem is, by nearly every measure, one of BioWare’s biggest failures — a critically savaged live-service shooter that EA shut down support for in 2021 after a planned full relaunch didn’t happen. And yet even reviews that tore the rest of the game apart singled out one thing: flying. Tom's Guide's review listed "awesome flight controls" as one of the game's only real pros. Piloting a Javelin exosuit means diving straight from open sky into an underwater cave with zero loading screens, banking and boosting with a sense of worth-it cathartic momentum few games have matched since.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3541. Godzilla Minus Zero Shuts Down One Of The Biggest Criticisms Of The Franchise

This article contains light spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

Godzilla has enjoyed a lasting popularity over his 70+ year existence, and it's no surprise. Ishirō Honda's 1954 "Godzilla" not only had a great title creature, but also involved a surprisingly weighty human drama that combined a love triangle with huge ethical conundrums, all of which fed into the film's impressively deep thematic material. It's a killer mixture, and Honda's movie is still thought of as one of the best movies ever made in the franchise all these years later. Although Toho Studios didn't immediately push the series towards bigger spectacle, the "Godzilla" films naturally took that course. Each successive film began creating bigger monster attack setpieces, and generated greater destruction by pitting the various monsters against each other.

This direction left any human characters with less screen time and importance in each movie. As such, the various writers and directors began to treat them more as perfunctory protagonists. While there have been several attempts to course correct this, it's a problem that persists. Even the MonsterVerse films have fallen prey to the common criticism that the human characters are second-rate.

This is part of why Takashi Yamazaki's "Godzilla Minus One" felt like such a breath of fresh air. That movie features a human story that is undeniably the core of the film, with Godzilla being more of a supporting feature. That approach continues in the sequel, "Godzilla Minus Zero," which doubles down on the great character work "Minus One" did by continuing the stories of already established characters, while also adding a few great new ones.

To be fair, there have been many prior movies in the "Godziilla" franchise that have featured some really compelling human characters and storylines to go with them. A few which leap to mind are "Godzilla vs. Biollante," "Godzilla vs. Destoroyah," and "Shin Godzilla." What these movies do well is find characters and a story that isn't completely based around attacks by Godzilla or other giant monsters, meaning that the characters are as proactive as they are reactive. When the latter becomes their primary function, the movies themselves essentially train the audience to not care about the humans as much, teaching them to wait patiently until the next big action scene occurs. In this way, the issues that some "Godzilla" movies have aren't all that different from a similar problem many genre movies face.

Where Takashi Yamazaki transcends this issue in "Godzilla Minus Zero" is in the way that he creates dramatic tension between the characters and Godzilla (or, in the film's case, Ghidorah) appearing. We the audience wish to see the giant monsters we came for, but Yamazaki's story positions many of these people as those who would likely be worse off should they turn up. Scientist Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka) is barely keeping a still-hurting Japan's head above water post World War II, let alone having to deal with kaiju attacks. The continued existence of Ghidorah is a personal burden to meterologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), while Godzilla's abilities present a dark temptation to professor Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka). Meanwhile, Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who found his will to live in "Minus One," is struggling like mad to keep his family together. Yet in addition to caring for adopted daughter Akiko (Saw Nagatani), his wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe) has been infected with Godzillas cells, which may end up killing her or could be used in other ways. The tension between wanting to see Godzilla and not wanting these people to suffer as a result is what Yamazaki exploits so beautifully.

One of the most impressive aspects of "Godzilla Minus Zero" is its restraint. As a big-budget direct sequel to the very successful "Godzilla Minus One," it would've made sense for Takashi Yamazaki and his crew to go bigger with the film's visual effects. The temptation to do this must've been especially great considering that "Minus One" won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects, making it the first "Godzilla" film ever to win an Oscar. Given that triumph, it's actually rather remarkable that Yamazaki didn't turn "Minus Zero" into a VFX extravaganza.

Instead, Yamazaki appears to deeply understand what makes visual effects great, which is their ability to enhance an already good story and its characters. The action sequences in "Minus Zero" are memorable because of how uniquely designed they are and how they utilize the characters. Moments like Shikishima flying through a village that's been upended by Ghidorah's gravity beam and Noda having to race against time to spring a trap on Ghidorah are made better because of the characters being directly involved in the action, not just observing.

All of this is why the big climax of "Godzilla Minus Zero" has relatively little to do with Godzilla and Ghidorah and is mostly to do with the fates of the human characters themselves. In a lesser movie, such scenes would feel like an obligatory denouement. in "Minus Zero," they're as riveting as anything else in the film. It may have taken over 70 years, but "Godzilla" has indeed finally circled back to where it began: a human drama that happens to feature a giant monster (charismatic as he may be).

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3540. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3539. Test Footage Of Clayface's Suit Just Arrived Online, And I Can't Look Away

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SPOILERS ahead for Clayface, now playing in theaters. Read ahead at your own risk.

It’s been a couple of weeks since Clayface officially debuted, and I can’t stop thinking about THAT ending and how Matt Hagen looks in the final minutes of the movie. I’d been wondering the whole film how a live-action Clayface would look, and I think it really delivered. However, I just found out that Clayface was created in real life for test footage.

CGI Clayface couldn’t hurt us, but a suit was really made, and it might haunt my nightmares now (complimentary)! Take a look below:

CLAYFACE suit in motion 👀 New BTS footage shows Spencer Wilding moving in the practical suit built by KM Effects. Fun fact: Spencer also played Kilowog on set in 2011's GREEN LANTERN. 🎥 KM Effects Ltd. https://t.co/UcnWD9nkKFNovember 6, 2026

I can’t stop looking at this, and with every glance I’m haunted further. This is pretty much how we see Matt Hagen in his final form; he’s just more clay colored in the movie. The suit was shared by KM Effects, which has also done the practical effects for Supergirl, Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom, The Flash and many more blockbusters.

Actor and stunt performer Spencer Wilding put the suit on to help out with on-set lighting and to provide texture references for the VFX team. Since the final Clayface was made from VFX, I didn't imagine a real-life suit being out there, but it makes so much sense to me now. Of course they’d need a reference to make Clayface look as life-like as possible. And, well… it's horrifying.

When CinemaBlend spoke to Clayface director James Watkins, he said that he spent a lot of time pondering every detail in order to cause the most impact for the last moments of the film. In his words:

I spent a lot of time thinking about and obsessing about his eye and his pain and how we can relate to his pain. I spent a lot of time focusing on the quality of his scream, his power of pain and the horror within that.

I imagine there were loads of different sketches and iterations of Clayface before this suit arrived, because it definitely isn’t the easiest comic book character to adapt into live-action. The movie marks DC’s first time making a comic book movie for horror fans, and they absolutely gave us all the body horror moments. Watkins even told us one obscure film from the genre he was inspired by.

Clayface may have faced polarizing reviews, but audiences like me really seemed to like it. The movie even earned an A- CinemaScore, a grade that’s very rare among horror movies.

Now that Clayface’s true form has been revealed, I have to wonder if he’ll show up in future DC movies. And is that suit lying around somewhere? I’m going to be honest here: I’m kind of stressed out about its existence now that I’ve seen it in all its creepy glory.

#3538. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3537. Gilligan's Island Star Jim Backus Voiced One Of Animation's Most Famous Characters

Though he may not be a household name today, Jim Backus was a well known character actor in the mid-20th Century. Of course, his most recognizable role will forever remain Thurston Howell III from "Gilligan's Island," as Backus brought a suitably refined energy to the part of a New England patrician stranded alongside other societal archetypes in the South Pacific. But Backus' career stretched far beyond three seasons of a beloved CBS sitcom. Both prior to and after becoming trapped on the Isle, for instance, he voiced the animated character Quincy Magoo, better known as Mr. Magoo — a role he played from 1949 until 1977.

The actor's pre-Thurston Howell career was already impressive. Before "Gilligan's Island," Backus appeared opposite Clint Eastwood in the movie "Francis in the Navy," although he gained far more in the way of significant recognition for putting on an acting masterclass as the Stark family patriarch, Frank Stark, in the James Dean classic "Rebel Without a Cause." That likely would've gone down as his biggest non-"Gilligan's Island" role, too, if it weren't for the fact he voiced Mr. Magoo for some three decades.

Like Thurston Howell, Mr. Magoo was a millionaire. Unlike Thurston Howell, however, this deep-pocketed, diminutive magnate had a severe case of near-sightedness — a condition he refused to acknowledge. Created by Millard Kaufman and John Hubley for the animation studio United Productions of America, Mr. Magoo first appeared in the 1949 theatrical short "The Ragtime Bear," which became a hit and ensured the character would stick around for a truly incredible amount of time. Indeed, the most recent "Mr. Magoo" cartoon ended in 2023, well after Backus had passed away. Still, he did voice the character for his first 30-ish years, arguably making Mr. Magoo Backus' most important role.

In a piece for Cinema Journal title "Memories of Mr. Magoo" (via JSTOR), producer Howard Rieder recalled how, long before Jim Backus' casting caused rewrites on "Gilligan's Island," the actor came to be hired for "The Ragtime Bear." It seems co-creator John Hubley asked actor Jerry Hausner, who voiced the character of Mr. Magoo's nephew and frequent sidekick Waldo, to help him find a suitable star. According to Rieder, Hausner remembered that Backus had arrived from New York where he was voicing the haughty playboy Hubert Updike III as part of the radio series "The Alan Young Show." It seems the actor was playing snooty millionaires long before he set foot on Gilligan's Isle.

According to Hausner's recollection, Backus was "fairly well-known" as the voice of Updike, and he seemed perfect for the voice of Mr. Magoo. "We had been friends for over 20 years," recalled Hausner (via Rieder). "I spoke to Hubley about Backus, and he wanted to meet him." Evidently, Backus was already well-established by this point, and Hubley didn't want to make him audition. Instead, he took him to the UPA studios and showed him character designs and storyboards. There, Backus found a personal connection to the character. As Hausner explained:

"He said, 'My father lives in his own little world, never quite seeing things the way they really are. It isn't that he's nearsighted, but his whole attitude toward life is a kind of personal isolation toward the rest of the world.' Backus mentioned that he used to do a character called the Man in the Club Car. It was the character of the businessman, the tycoon, the loudmouth talker [...] He began to use this voice and it was the voice that ultimately became Mr. Magoo."

After making his debut as Mr. Magoo in "The Ragtime Bear," Jim Backus went on to voice the character in multiple theatrical cartoons and the 1960s syndicated TV series "Mister Magoo." He returned to voice the character in multiple TV specials, along with two follow-up series: "The Famous Adventures of Mr. Magoo," which aired between 1964 and '65, and "What's New, Mr. Magoo?" in 1977.

Over the course of his multiple films and series, the character evolved from a mean-spirited, irascible toff to a senescent, lovable buffoon. The comedy arose from his inability to recognize the often precarious and dangerous situations into which he frequently stumbled due to his near-sightedness. And while those around him were perpetually stressed by his near-misses, due to sheer luck, Mr. Magoo always seemed to come out unscathed.

Backus gave voice to this miraculously lucky millionaire right up until the end of "What's New, Mr. Magoo?" in 1977 — the year before he returned as Thurston Howell III for one of the three "Gilligan's Island" TV movies, "Rescue from Gilligan's Island." Unfortunately, the actor was in bad health by the time he made a brief cameo appearance in 1981's "The Harlem Globetrotters on Gilligan's Island," and he passed away in 1989.

Mr. Magoo, however, endured. Not only did the Backus-voiced version remain part of popular culture via syndication deals, Leslie Nielsen played the character in an ill-fated 1997 live-action film that became a box office disappointment and debuted to negative reviews. More recently, a French animated series, "Mr. Magoo," began airing in 2019 and lasted until 2023.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3533. John Goodman Thinks He Shouldn't Have Starred In George Clooney's 2014 Critical Flop

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

George Clooney enjoys a heightened status in Hollywood. He is one of the most handsome and charismatic movie stars in the history of the medium, and he relishes the opportunity to make a total fool out of himself (especially if he's working for Joel and Ethan Coen). For a moment, his instincts were unerring. On the strength of "Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" and "Good Night, and Good Luck," those instincts seemed to extend to directing. His next two directorial efforts, "Leatherheads" and "The Ides of March," were solid, but they lacked the snap of his early work. Then he just up and lost it.

Clooney's last five movies — "The Monuments Men," "Suburbicon," "The Midnight Sky," "The Tender Bar" and "The Boys in the Boat" — are bizarrely inert. I revere Clooney as an actor (I wrote a book about him), and, via interviews with people who know him well, believe that he cares deeply about his art. But there's no passion in those aforementioned movies. They're smart, considered, compassionate works, but they've got a blasé point of view. Clooney admirably promotes a humanistic point of view, but there's no technical or intellectual rigor behind his efforts. It's like watching LeBron James make layups.

I hate writing this stuff because I know Clooney has it in him to make great films. But when I run into a series of comments from a serious actor like John Goodman about how he spent months working on "The Monuments Men" with Clooney, only to walk away wishing he hadn't made the movie, I wonder where it all went wrong. While Goodman admittedly had a good time making the film, he also confessed, "It was one of those movies ... I probably shouldn't have done."

During a recent SAG-AFTRA Foundation Q&A, Goodman dished on two films that, in his estimation, he shouldn't have done. One was John Landis' reviled "Saturday Night Live" movie sequel "Blues Brothers 2000," which at least gave the rhythm and blues aficionado the opportunity to work with music legends like Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett, and B.B. King. He didn't mention Landis' involvement in the deaths of Vic Morrow, Myca Dinh Le, and Renee Shin-Ye Lee on the set of "Twilight Zone: The Movie," but people were still making films with the director at the time.

The other was "The Monuments Men" with Clooney. According to Goodman, "George loves movies and he loves stories and he's such a great storyteller himself, and I think he's a great director. I had fun with him. 'Monuments Men.' We were over in Germany for six months. And England."

But the film about art experts being dropped into Europe during World War II to save the continent's cultural treasures was DOA critically and commercially. It's a handsomely mounted would-be epic, but the theme is clearly stated early on, which leaves Clooney nowhere to go narratively. Protecting art, reinforcing its importance in the middle of a war that threatens to end civilization, is a wildly worthwhile premise. Especially now. I just wish Clooney and co-screenwriter Grant Heslov hadn't taken a softball approach to this subject. We need a guy like Clooney hurling heat.

#3531. Walter Koenig Wanted A Star Trek: The Next Generation Role That Wasn't Pavel Chekov

While "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is set 100 years after "Star Trek: The Original Series," some "TOS" cast members appeared on the show. In the pilot, "Encounter at Farpoint," a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) visits the Enterprise-D and gives Data (Brent Spiner) some sound advice: "You treat her like a lady, she'll always bring you home."

Later, in the Season 3 episode "Sarek," Mark Lenard guest-starred as the eponymous Vulcan ambassador, also known for being Spock's (Leonard Nimoy) father. Spock himself then appeared in the Season 5 two-parter "Reunification," where it's revealed he's moved to Romulus to try and bring the Vulcans and Romulans together again as one. After that, the former Enterprise Chief Engineer Scotty (James Doohan) appeared in the "Next Generation" Season 6 Episode "Relics," having spent several decades trapped in a Dyson sphere. Finally, Captain Kirk (William Shatner) teamed up with Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) in the 1994 spin-off film "Star Trek Generations."

That lineup leaves out George Takei (Sulu), Nichelle Nichols (Uhura), and Walter Koenig (Chekov), who died this past October right before Stewart did. The closest Koenig came to appearing on "The Next Generation" was in "Star Trek: Generations." In a scene set in 2294, Captain Kirk, Scotty, and Chekov attend the maiden voyage of the Enterprise-B. But Koenig had a pitch to appear on "Next Generation," which he shared in the October 1989 issue of "Starlog" magazine:

"I don't want to do a walk-on. I have an idea for an opening moment. Somebody has just come aboard the ship. They're talking about him in general. He turns around and it's [my] face. They say, 'Well, Commander Chekov.' 'No,' I say, 'Lt. Commander Chekov, Pavel Chekov's son.' It's a great opening."

"Star Trek" is no stranger at all to reusing the same actors to play different roles, including across series. Majel Barrett (wife of "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry), who played Nurse Chapel on the original series, also had a recurring part on "Next Generation" as Ambassador Lwaxana Troi, mother of Counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

It's worth noting that Walter Koenig specifically wanted a part worth playing — "Not a walk-on" as he put it. Joining "Star Trek" in Season 2, Chekov was invariably the most overlooked member of the cast. One of his biggest parts in the "Trek" movies was in "Wrath of Khan," and that whole role is built on a continuity error: Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán) and Chekov know each other even though Koenig wasn't part of the "Star Trek" cast during Khan's first appearance, "Space Seed." Koenig later claimed he caught the error but, tellingly, stayed silent to protect his screentime.

Koenig often said he preferred his role on "Babylon 5," a different sci-fi series where he played the sinister psychic Alfred Bester, over playing Chekov because Bester was a much more substantive role. Note that "Starlog" interview was in 1989, years before "Babylon 5," so it's no surprise he was hungry for meaty roles.

"Star Trek: Picard" Season 3 eventually used Koenig's idea to give him a voiceover cameo as Anton Chekov, son of Pavel and the Federation's president. ("Anton" doubles as a homage to the late Anton Yelchin, who played Chekov in the 2009 "Star Trek" film and its sequels.) Sadly, though, that sort of Easter Egg cameo is exactly the kind of appearance Koenig had said he didn't want to settle for back in 1989.

#3530. James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009

James Gray time-travels back to his Queens roots once again for his latest film, “Paper Tiger.” It’s a location, an atmosphere, a state of mind he’s explored across decades and genres, dating back to his 1994 debut feature, “Little Odessa.” Like “Paper Tiger,” “Little Odessa” also featured the shadows of the Russian mafia looming over a family unit — to devastating ends. But even 30-plus years later, with his new movie — starring Miles Teller, Adam Driver, and Scarlett Johansson — Gray wanted to go just as dangerous.

Adam Driver, for one, has danger in him, according to Gray, who cast the Oscar nominee as a former police officer who links up with the red mafia in the 1980s. Gray recently joined IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio for a wide-ranging, amusingly discursive live conversation at the Virginia Film Festival. One that showcased his knack for impressions — from Luca Guadagnino beckoning Gray out of this year’s Cannes to sit down for the Italian filmmaker’s Bernardo Bertolucci documentary, to the waves of disappointment cresting through Maximilian Schell during an early Venice screening of “Little Odessa.” Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Almost all great performances have to have some measure of danger in them,” Gray said. “I can actually only think of one that doesn’t have any, which would probably be Jeff Bridges as The Dude in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ which has no danger at all.” (Though John Goodman’s PTSD-addled Vietnam vet in the Coens’ 1998 hardboiled slacker comedy qualifies as dangerous.)

“Adam is a fantastic, intense presence in [‘Paper Tiger’],” said Gray, who wrote “Paper Tiger” with Driver in mind.

Gray also spoke about the “recurring nightmares” for any filmmaker: “You screen your movie, and everybody walks out midway through. I’ve never had that happen to me, thank God.”

But one personal experience of watching this happen to someone else became seared in his unconscious: “When I was on the jury in Cannes [in 2009] … there was a movie made by a fantastic director. I won’t say his name, but he’s a great director of real reputation. And you have to sit in this jury box, which is sort of in the back of a theater, and the seats … when a person gets up, it’s spring-activated, and so it makes this very loud tack. I’m on the jury, and I’m watching this movie, and I start hearing tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack. And people start walking out in droves. And the movie ended, and it was about half full, and people were booing. And that did become a nightmare for me. And by the way, I’m not the only director for whom that’s a nightmare. I’ve talked to many director friends of mine, and they’re like, ‘Oh, yeah. No, I’ve had that dream.'”

James Gray served on the Cannes jury in 2009 under president Isabelle Huppert — whom he reiterated, as Huppert previously did with IndieWire, he has no feud with despite rumors of a fractious deliberation — with such films as Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void” and Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist” in the competition. (But again, he’s not naming names here.)

“I know there’s directors who go, ‘I like it. I like when they boo,’ but that’s such a crock,” said Gray. We also asked for his thoughts on audiences dozing off in movies — which some directors, like Lucrecia Martel, have likened to falling asleep in the sun, a reflex of comfort — which certainly happens with some frequency at Cannes as any attendee knows.

“Who likes when you fall asleep during a movie? No, I’m sorry. The movie is required to keep you awake, and as Hitchcock once said, it has to be just long enough to accommodate your bladder’s capacity,” Gray said. “Which, by the way, you know when people say, ‘Oh, well, what do you think of the streaming thing and all that?’ I have only one real beef with streaming, and that’s the pause button, because it is my job to keep you there for an hour and a half, two hours, maybe even three. Where you’re not falling asleep, where you are riveted, where you’re not moving.”

He added, “I can’t stand the people who go, ‘I watched the first half on Tuesday, but I’m gonna catch the second half on a Saturday.’ … There’s nothing you can do about it, and it’s not, it’s not streamer-centered, because most people watch your films now at home. And whether it’s Netflix or Peacock or whatever, it doesn’t matter. The pause button is a problem.”

He pointed to his early relationship to “Vertigo,” a Hitchcock film he didn’t like in the first half, as an example of the virtues of experiencing a movie entirely in one sitting. “The result is so much more rewarding when you are forced to experience the whole thing because it’s like a dream, and you can’t pause your dream. And sometimes you don’t like your dream … sometimes the only way you can get yourself out of that dream is to convince yourself it is a dream in your dream. REM sleep is an hour and a half to two hours a night. What’s a movie’s runtime? It’s about the same thing. It didn’t happen by accident,” Gray said.
