#3511. 8 DC Heroes Who Would Be Better Green Lanterns Than Fans Expect

The Green Lantern Ring is one of the universe’s most powerful weapons, and the Guardians choose their champions based on their ability to overcome great fear. While iconic Green Lanterns such as Hal Jordan and John Stewart are worthy wielders of the ring, the allure of wondering how other heroes would fare is far too great.

The DC universe is full of heroes with the right psychological profiles and traits to make fantastic Green Lanterns. Willpower isn’t in short supply in DC, but some heroes are so fearless, mentally resilient, and willful that they could be even better Green Lanterns than fans realise right away.

This article spotlights eight heroes who would make better Green Lanterns than fans might expect. From street-level heroes to some of DC’s heaviest hitters, these unsung figures have exactly the traits needed to master the ring. They are already formidable, but a Green Lantern ring would unlock an entirely new layer of their potential.

Batman uses fear to keep criminals in check, which makes him a strong candidate for a Yellow Lantern ring, but fans may also not expect the Dark Knight to become a powerful Green Lantern. The animated series The Batman (2004) shows how effective he would be with the ring.

In the series, after Sinestro attacks him, Hal Jordan sends his ring to Gotham City to find Batman. Although the ring initially falls into the Penguin’s hands, it eventually reaches Batman. With the ring on a low charge, Batman fights and defeats Sinestro, showing he is adept at using the Green Lantern ring.

Overall, Batman is one of DC’s best strategists, a master of all kinds of combat, and an extremely disciplined crime fighter. With a lantern ring, Batman can put his strategic mind to good use, turning the ring into the ultimate tactical weapon. When it comes to sheer willpower, very few heroes can match the Caped Crusader.

The Green Lantern Corps has never lacked power, but it has often lacked wisdom at the top. The Guardians have repeatedly made poor decisions with potentially devastating consequences, including creating the Manhunters. As a result, Diana of Themyscira would not only be a powerful addition to the Corps, but also a great leader.

Diana has commanded Amazon armies, anchored the Justice League through its darkest crises, and served as an ambassador between gods and mortals. She is as wise as she is powerful, and her skills would be best used leading the Green Lantern Corps as a member.

Beyond her outstanding leadership and strategic mind, she is also a fierce warrior and a compassionate hero. Diana is a proud Amazon warrior, and bravery and willpower abound on Themyscira. With a Green Lantern ring, she transforms from a hero who can hold her own against Superman into one of the most powerful Green Lanterns.

John Constantine is nothing if not creative. His unprecedented ability to think on his feet and battle powerful otherworldly threats makes him a top-tier Green Lantern. Constantine’s entire career is defined by staring down literal demons, hellish overlords, and cosmic horrors while armed with nothing but raw nerve. It’s not that he’s fearless; he’s just immensely courageous.

His occult expertise could become twice as dangerous when combined with a Lantern ring. His mind could generate ethereal binding runes, hard-light sigils, and metaphysical cages. He could also create devastating constructs of powerful demons and otherworldly beings, crafting intricate esoteric constructs designed specifically to exploit his opponent’s psychological and mystical weaknesses.

Giving a Speedster a Green Lantern ring basically makes them unstoppable. That is even more true when the Speedster is the Flash. Whether it is Barry Allen or Wally West, the Speed Force demands incredible mental fortitude to wield properly. The Flash sees most things in slow motion, giving him plenty of time to create ideal constructs.

Pairing the Green Lantern ring’s ability to operate at the speed of thought with the Flash’s faster-than-light speed thinking means a Flash with a ring could generate millions of unique hard-light constructs instantly. The Flash would have ample time to create constructs that defy the imagination before his enemies can process what is happening.

A Green Lantern ring is limited only by its wielder’s imagination, which makes Jaime Reyes a perfect candidate. The Blue Beetle scarab works much like the Green Lantern ring: it reads intent and creates weapons the user can imagine. Giving Jaime a ring would not only be a power-up, but it’s right in his wheelhouse.

Furthermore, Jaime’s life is defined by constantly resisting the scarab’s lethal programming and standing his ground against cosmic threats. Overcoming the fear of losing control of his body shows immense willpower, but his real advantage is his bond with extraterrestrial technology, which would give his constructs an unimaginable edge.

Instead of generating static shields or basic blades, his mind would produce dynamic, evolving weaponry that mirrors Reach tech. His constructs would instantly adapt to target vulnerabilities, morphing mid-battle, making him a deadly combination of human creativity and machine logic.

When fans think of Raven, they immediately picture shadow magic and the dark, demonic influence of her father, Trigon. However, her entire life has been a constant exercise in mental discipline and emotional control. Holding back absolute evil from consuming her soul takes astonishing willpower, proving her mind is stronger than most people imagine.

Her unique psychological training would give her constructs an unprecedented edge. Coupled with her mastery of magic, Raven would make a uniquely terrifying Green Lantern, able to turn nightmares into reality through powerful constructs. Her intense focus, sharpened by years of keeping inner turmoil at bay, would produce constructs of rare density and absolute stability.

Mister Miracle’s whole existence is defined by resisting the overwhelming, soul-crushing terror of Darkseid and the pits of Apokolips. With impeccable escape artistry and unshakable willpower, he did the unthinkable and escaped Darkseid’s prison and grasp. For Scott Free, surrendering to fear was never an option; his unbreakable determination to break every chain makes him a natural fit for willpower.

Moreover, a Green Lantern ring lets the user turn raw imagination into hard-light constructs, and Scott’s mind is uniquely suited to construct creation. Having mastered every escape technique in the cosmos, Mister Miracle has a creative mind that would lend itself to devastating, intricate constructs.

While Superman is a Symbol of Hope in the DC universe, he also has incredible willpower and is an ideal candidate for a Green Lantern ring. The core requirement of a Green Lantern is not just possessing willpower, but the ability to overcome great fear, and Superman has this in abundance.

The Man of Steel may have unimaginable power; he routinely faces beings strong enough to kill him, such as Darkseid and Doomsday. He never backs away from a confrontation when the world is in danger. Moreover, with a super-genius-level intellect and super-speed cognition, he can create highly detailed and creative constructs.

Furthermore, willpower powers the ring and determines how solid the constructs are. Superman’s willpower and mental discipline, sharpened through years of controlling his immense powers, would make him an incredibly powerful Green Lantern. Earth Green Lanterns usually protect Sector 2814, but Superman already does that and more every day.

#3510. 10 Perfectly Designed Final Fantasy Magic Cards That Are 10/10, No Notes

A critical hit of Final Fantasy nostalgia

Magic: The Gathering's Final Fantasy crossover set is a love letter to one of gaming's most enduring franchises, bringing together characters, creatures, locations, and iconic moments from across the series' history. With 16 mainline games and even more when counting sequels and spinoffs, Wizards of the Coast had quite the challenge in translating decades of RPG storytelling into a card game with its own language and mechanics.

Packed with hilarious nods, like Suplex, and incredible powerhouses, like Diamond Weapon, it comes as no surprise that Final Fantasy is among the best Universe Beyond sets in the game. But the most perfect designs among them capture a fundamental element of their source material, whether that's Bahamut's devastating Mega Flare, Phoenix Down's clutch resurrection, or the sheer spectacle of summoning Primal Odin.

Whether through clever mechanics or an inspired bit of flavor, these 10 Final Fantasy cards represent the very best of what this crossover has to offer.

Sin anchors the legacy of Final Fantasy antagonists through crushing generational dread, and its card design captures that weight without relying on a lazy stat line. Whenever Sin, Spira's Punishment enters the battlefield or attacks, it exiles a random permanent card from your graveyard, creating a tapped token copy if it's a permanent and repeating the process if a land is hit. Sin is particularly nasty in Commander decks built around graveyard recursion and land synergies, especially when paired with cards like Adrix and Nev, Twincasters, which doubles the tokens it creates, or Hedron Crab, which helps stock the graveyard with fresh targets.

It's an unpredictable engine that turns the remnants of your battlefield into compounding threats throughout the game. Spira’s Punishment also evokes the inescapable cycle of destruction and rebirth that defines Final Fantasy 10, where Spira's people have endured a thousand years of Sin's devastation, rebuilding their lives after each attack and relying on Summoners to temporarily defeat the monster through a ritual sacrifice. Even its seven-mana cost feels entirely appropriate for a monster of its magnitude, though maybe 10 would’ve been more apropos.

Weapons in gaming rarely carry the instant recognition of Cloud Strife's enormous Buster Sword — whether you picture it crudely strapped to his back during the bleak industrial sprawl of early Final Fantasy 7 or dragging it through the mud in Remake — but its significance extends well beyond its imposing silhouette. Passed down through Angeal, Zack, and eventually Cloud, the sword represents the heavy burden of legacy and what one generation leaves behind for another.

Magic: The Gathering captures some of that history through its equipment design, with the Buster Sword giving its wielder a substantial power boost of +3/+2. Whenever said creature hits an opponent directly, you draw a card, then get the opportunity to cast a spell from your hand for free, provided its mana value doesn't exceed the damage dealt. It's a suitably devastating reward for landing a direct hit, and a fitting tribute to one of Final Fantasy's most enduring symbols.

At first glance, Cactuars look like little more than walking houseplants, but when crossed, they can hit you with a devastating flurry of needles. Among Final Fantasy's most recognizable recurring monsters, Cactuars have made a career out of looking harmless before delivering some devastating blows, similar to the goofy-looking Tonberries. MTG’s Jumbo Cactuar follows that lineage beautifully through a seven-mana creature with a relatively unassuming 1/7 stat line. It looks like any regular green common creature, until you notice its ability, 10,000 Needles, which gives it a whopping +9,999/+0 whenever it attacks.

That's right, this seemingly harmless plant suddenly becomes a 10,000-power monster capable of flattening just about anything in its path. It's an almost comically literal interpretation of the Cactuar family's signature attack, and that's what makes it so brilliant (and hilarious). There's no need for elaborate transformations or complicated synergies. Magic simply takes one of Final Fantasy's most recognizable monster abilities and turns it into a devastating combat trick.

While Final Fantasy 13 remains one of the most divisive entries in the franchise’s storied history, Lightning herself stands tall as one of its absolute finest protagonists. She’s a relentless soldier defined by unwavering resolve and immediate action, a former Guardian Corps sergeant who goes AWOL during the violent exile of Bodhum's citizens, derailing a Purge train and battling through the Hanging Edge to rescue her sister.

Her Magic card captures that uncompromising spirit right out of the gate. A three-mana creature with first strike, trample, and lifelink is already a formidable combatant, but her stagger ability is what makes the design sing. Whenever Lightning, Army of One deals combat damage to an opponent, all damage dealt to that player and their permanents by any source is doubled until your next turn. It’s a brilliant adaptation of FF13’s defining combat rhythm, where staggering an enemy leaves them completely exposed to devastating follow-up attacks. Magic turns her into the tip of the spear for an all-out assault, translating one of the series' signature mechanics into a game-winning tactical engine.

Zack Fair's story is one of Final Fantasy 7’s most heartbreaking, particularly because his final moments have such a profound impact on Cloud's journey. Magic honors the character with a 0/1 legendary creature that enters with a +1/+1 counter on it. You can play one mana to sacrifice Zack Fair and give another creature indestructible, Zack’s counters, and even the equipment attached to him.

It's a thoughtful piece of design that essentially turns his death into an act of protection and inheritance. There's no elaborate transformation or complicated combination of abilities, Zack's final act becomes a playable mechanic, allowing another hero to carry his strength and equipment forward. It’s hard to imagine a more poignant tribute to a character whose entire legacy is defined by passing the torch, and some players have found clever ways to abuse it by looping him from the graveyard with reanimation engines like Sun Titan or Lurrus, repeatedly granting their board indestructible while constantly passing his stat boosts down the line.

Aerith’s power has always stemmed from gentle resilience rather than overwhelming force. She’s a healer, after all, and the last surviving Cetra, hiding in plain sight selling flowers in the Sector 5 slums while carrying the solitary burden of the Planet's survival. In Magic, Aerith Gainsborough is a 2/2 legendary creature that enters the battlefield with lifelink, and whenever you gain life, she receives a +1/+1 counter. This makes her progressively stronger as she supports your other creatures and keeps your life total at a healthy advantage over your opponents.

However, the real stroke of genius comes when Aerith dies. Every legendary creature you control receives +1/+1 counters equal to the number Aerith had accumulated during her time on the battlefield. It's a beautiful mechanical interpretation of her legacy, particularly considering the profound impact her death has on Cloud and the rest of the party in the original game. Aerith's influence doesn't disappear when she's gone, but lives on through the people she leaves behind. And it’s even better when you’ve already got a 12/12 Eldrazi on the board.

Final Fantasy 10’s Yuna is a summoner first and foremost, making her one of the most natural candidates for a Magic card built around enchantments and their associated creatures. What makes Yuna, Hope of Spira particularly clever is how the card encourages players to assemble a collection of saga creatures, the special enchantments introduced in the Final Fantasy set to represent the franchise's iconic summons.

During your turn, Yuna grants herself and your other enchantment creatures trample, lifelink, and ward 2, making the entire group considerably more difficult to deal with. She can also return an enchantment from your graveyard to the battlefield at the end of your turn, but with a finality counter on it that prevents it from returning to the graveyard again. It's a fantastic representation of Yuna's role as a summoner, turning her into the centerpiece of an entire Aeon-focused strategy with enchantment creatures cards like Yojimbo, Bahamut, Knights of Round, and more.

Speaking of Knights of Round, it's as much a powerful Magic card as it is a legendary summon in the games. First appearing as the ultimate secret Materia in Final Fantasy 7, tucked away on the unmapped Round Island and requiring a Gold Chocobo just to reach, it calls forth 13 holy knights to rain down an unskippable two-minute-long assault of apocalyptic damage. It was the absolute pinnacle of endgame excess, forcing players to sit back and watch a cinematic spectacle unfold while Sephiroth’s health bar disintegrated.

Magic’s interpretation of it is every bit as theatrical. Designed as an eight-mana Saga creature, Knights of Round gradually builds an army by creating three 2/2 Knight tokens across each of its first four chapters. That’s twelve knights in total, before its fifth and final chapter delivers Ultimate End, buffing your entire board with +2/+2 and dropping an indestructible counter onto each of your creatures. It's a wonderfully patient piece of design that rewards players for waiting out the full summon sequence, turning that notoriously long animation into a looming, game-ending countdown your opponents can only watch in dread. Unless they’re in blue, of course.

Sephiroth’s transformation from celebrated First Class SOLDIER hero to the cold One-Winged Angel remains one of gaming’s most devastating character arcs. He wasn't just a villain; he was Shinra's ultimate hero whose sanity shattered the moment he uncovered his horrific origins inside the Nibelheim mansion: he was engineered from the alien calamity Jenova. He burned Nibelheim to the ground and began viewing humanity as mere parasites. His tragic fall shifted the entire scope of Final Fantasy 7 from an anti-corporate resistance story into an apocalyptic cosmic horror.

Magic imbues that journey onto a double-faced creature that grows more dangerous as the battlefield descends into chaos. On his front side, Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER allows you to sacrifice another creature whenever he enters or attacks, drawing a card in return. Meanwhile, whenever another creature dies, you drain one life from an opponent and gain one yourself. Once that second ability has resolved for the fourth time in a single turn, Sephiroth transforms into his One-Winged Angel form, granting an emblem that keeps the life-drain engine running permanently whenever creatures die. You can also even stack that with his second ability, letting you sac as many creatures as you like in exchange for that many card draws. It's an inspired way to represent Sephiroth's growing power, turning the battlefield into a ticking clock as his enemies fall around him.

Final Fantasy 11 has no shortage of formidable enemies, but few developed the same legendary reputation as Absolute Virtue. This optional superboss became infamous for its extraordinary durability and punishing difficulty, earning a reputation as one of the most frustrating encounters in the entire franchise. Absolute Virtue could repeatedly unleash powerful abilities borrowed from multiple player classes, including Benediction, which allowed it to restore enormous amounts of health just when victory seemed within reach. Its substantial passive regeneration made matters even worse, turning the encounter into an exhausting war of attrition that demanded meticulous coordination from an entire alliance of players. Some groups spent more than 18 hours attempting to defeat it, cementing its place in MMO history as one of gaming's most notorious boss encounters.

Magic distills its intimidating presence through an eight-mana 8/8 construction that can't be countered when it’s played, plus it has flying, of course. Even more terrifying is its secondary ability, which grants you protection from each of your opponents, effectively making you untouchable while Absolute Virtue remains on the battlefield. Opponents can’t attack you, target you with spells, or even enchant you. It's a fitting translation of a boss that once seemed practically impossible to defeat, forcing opponents to find a way around its defenses before they can even think about bringing it down.

#3509. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us onFacebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

#3508. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3507. 10 Sci-Fi Books To Read Before Kicking the Bucket

Thankfully, for people who love science fiction literature, we're talking about one of the most diverse and prolific genres in all of speculative fiction, making it so that there are hundreds upon hundreds of sci-fi masterpieces out there for them to explore. There are ten particular books, however, that absolutely everyone who enjoys science fiction should read before kicking the bucket, the most essential cornerstones that the genre has to offer.

Whether we're talking about a foundational modern classic, like Neuromancer, or an even older watershed moment in the genre's history, like The War of the Worlds, these are books so important, influential, marvelously written, and pop-culturally relevant that they should be considered must-read material. Even people who think they don't like science fiction should give these gems a chance.

You need to be a really important name to get an entire literary award carrying your name, and there's nothing that Arthur C. Clarke was if not massively important. Many would point to Rendezvous with Rama, the first installment in the Rama series, as the author's magnum opus. One of the most perfect sci-fi books set in space, it's about a human crew who intercepts and explores a massive alien starship that enters the solar system, only for the vessel to depart without ever making contact with humanity.

Winner of all the Hugo, Locus, and Nebula Awards—a tremendous achievement not accomplished by many—, Rendezvous with Rama is the definitive blueprint for the "Big Dumb Object" (BDO) subgenre of sci-fi, which is all about the discovery of mysterious alien structures. It's an essential hard sci-fi narrated with a sense of wonder that perfectly captures the natural thrill of discovery and exploration.

William Gibson's Neuromancer remains the first and only novel in history ever to win all three of the Hugo, Nebula, and Philip K. Dick Awards, and for good reason. It's the first installment in the Sprawl trilogy, but this novel about a hacker who's recruited to help a rogue AI merge with its sibling and achieve supreme power is best known as the most important pioneer of the cyberpunk subgenre.

With its exploration of themes of AI and humanity's relationship with technology, Neuromancer is also one of the most prophetic sci-fi books of all time, making it even more essential reading than it already was before. It's a cultural blueprint unlike any other, inventing much of the language of the digital age and building the aesthetics of a sci-fi subgenre that has delivered several of the greatest sci-fi stories across all forms of media.

Another one of the most important and massively influential sci-fi authors in history was Philip K. Dick, whose dystopian sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? inspired Ridley Scott's Blade Runner, itself one of those sci-fi movies that everyone should watch at least once in their lives. The book is set on a futuristic Earth, where a bounty hunter is tasked with hunting down a group of rogue human-like androids.

The question of what it means to be human is one that has been explored by science fiction since the genre's birth, but rarely has that theme been explored with as much psychological and philosophical depth as in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? It's one of the greatest sci-fi book masterpieces in history, essential reading for all those who are even remotely interested in this common thematic concern for science fiction.

Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 is one of the most influential dystopian novels in the history of science fiction, following a book burner who rebels against an oppressive society, which sparks a journey of intellectual awakening and survival. It's one of the most essential sci-fi classics to read before kicking the bucket, a razor-sharp commentary on mass media, censorship, and anti-intellectualism.

While other dystopian writers who either influenced Bradbury or were his direct contemporaries wrote about government surveillance or the dangers of hedonism, Fahrenheit 451 is all about a society that willingly abandons deep thought in favor of cheap, fast entertainment. As such, few dystopian books feel as timely as this one; and as such, Fahrenheit 451 couldn't possibly feel any more essential.

H. G. Wells was one of the most important and influential figures in the history of science fiction and modern literature, pioneering tropes like time travel, genetic engineering, and—of course—alien invasions. Indeed, there's perhaps no alien invasion novel more foundational than The War of The Worlds, in which a dying Martian civilization launches a devastating invasion of southern England despite the human military's best efforts to keep them at bay.

It's one of those sci-fi masterpieces that became a blueprint for the whole sci-fi genre, and even though its pacing and sociological musings may feel somewhat archaic to today's readers, its entertaining value is still every bit as sharp and fresh as it surely must have been back in 1898. Full of biting social commentary and memorable moments, it's a masterpiece so hugely influential that no true fan of science fiction can allow themselves to kick the bucket before experiencing Wells' brilliance.

Isaac Asimov's Foundation series is another one of the most important sci-fi book series of all time, but most people would agree that it's also one of those book series that peaked with their first entry. The eponymous Foundation is a cycle of five interrelated short stories, telling the early story of the titular institute and its mission to preserve the best of galactic civilization after the collapse of the Galactic Empire.

...The best possible introduction to the oeuvre of an author who's easily among the most influential in the history of science fiction.

One of those sci-fi books that are perfect from start to finish, Foundation is the best possible introduction to the oeuvre of an author who's easily among the most influential in the history of science fiction. It's a tale of tremendous scale and unbelievable philosophical depth, setting a whole new gold standard for space operas whose effect can still be felt across the subgenre to this day. It's smart, it's deeply nuanced, and it's a love letter to old-school sci-fi as a whole.

Ursula K. Le Guin was one of the most central figures in the history of 20th-century speculative fiction, just as well-known for her fantasy masterpieces as she is for sci-fi gems like The Left Hand of Darkness. It's one of the best Hugo Award winners of all time, about a human sent to an ice-covered planet to persuade its genderless civilization to join an intergalactic alliance.

It was Le Guin's first hugely successful science fiction novel, instantly establishing her as a major voice in the genre. With it, Le Guin demonstrated that far from only being able to tell pulpy stories about fast-paced space adventures with fancy gadgets and spaceships, sci-fi could be genuine high art. A radically subversive thought experiment on themes as complex as gender, sexuality, and humanity itself, The Left Hand of Darkness fundamentally expanded readers' perception of what sci-fi could accomplish.

Many would very confidently say that Frank Herbert's Dune is the single greatest and most influential sci-fi novel of the 20th century, and it wouldn't be easy to disagree with them. This grand, thematically expansive space opera tells the story of young nobleman Paul Atreides, who survives a political betrayal on the desert planet of Arrakis and has to unite its indigenous people to embark on a destructive religious crusade for revenge.

The reason why Dune has been one of the highest-rated sci-fi books on Goodreads is that on top of being deeply influential, it's also genuinely flawless from cover to cover. Thanks to its patient pacing, its layered character writing, and its fascinatingly nuanced exploration of themes of ecology, politics, power, and religion, it has stood the test of time as one of the most artfully crafted masterpieces in the history of sci-fi literature.

There is perhaps no dystopian sci-fi novel better-known or more influential than George Orwell's 1984, where a low-level Party worker rebels against an all-seeing totalitarian regime. But though most readers may be used to stories of rebellion against oppression that have happy endings, this is one of the most hopeless books of all time, and that's exactly why it's so timeless.

Even after 77 years since its publication, 1984 deals with themes that feel terrifyingly prescient and all-too timely to modern times. But as if its prophetic nature weren't enough, it's also an impeccably-written masterpiece, having created much of the language that people still continue to use to analyze and discuss authoritarianism, propaganda, and the surveillance state.

Back in 1816, an 18-year-old Mary Shelley conceived and began writing Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. Two years later, the novel was published; and thus came to be the book that historians tend to agree marks the birth of science fiction as a genre. The foundations had been laid by other authors before, but it was this story about a young scientist bringing a stitched-together corpse to life that built the first true sci-fi story ever on top of those foundations.

Indeed, Shelley is the grandmother of sci-fi, and that means that there is no science fiction book more essential for anyone and everyone to read—including those who don't tend to love the genre—than Frankenstein. It's one of those classic horror books that are still perfect in 2026, an eternally entertaining and worthwhile read whose philosophical, artistic, and psychological depth has often been imitated and adapted, but never fully matched.

Dr. Pretorius attempts to find Frankenstein's monster, long believed dead, to further the scientific work started by Dr. Victor Frankenstein decades before.

#3506. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3505. ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases “Zi” in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

A Hong Kong violinist who’s losing her grip on reality, young Zi (Michelle Mao) is haunted by visions of her future self. The doctors at the local neurology center suspect that she might be suffering from the early symptoms of a brain tumor, but Zi — a being of pure cinema, cobbled together from the half-formed memories of films like “La Jetée” and “Cléo from 5 to 7” — will have to wait a long and lonely 24 hours for the test results to come back.  Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

Well, maybe not so lonely. Crying on one of the innumerable concrete steps that climb Lantau Island, Zi is consoled by a sweet American expat with a strangely familiar face (and an aggressively unnatural blonde wig). Her name is L, she’s a disillusioned former dancer played by the luminous Haley Lu Richardson, and she can’t help but reciprocate the inexplicable closeness that Zi feels towards her. Over the course of a single night together, these two lost souls will help to relocate each other in time — to resynchronize with the world around them, reconnect with the infinite potential of the present, and return themselves to the creative purpose that once anchored them to it.

Even if seen without a shred of context, it would be obvious to anyone that “Zi” was made by someone who is — or hopefully was — desperate to spark a realignment of his own. To steal himself away from regret and anxiety and tether his perspective back to the now. Shot without a script or a budget in the immediate aftermath of Kogonada’s ill-received “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” (the “After Yang” auteur’s studio debut, by all indications a soul-crushing experience for an artist whose two previous features retained the delicate grace of the video essays that he used to make), this searching and unformed wisp of an experiment hardly represents the first time that an ascendent director has scaled down after a misstep, but “Zi” takes the notion of “one for me” to much greater and more galvanizing extremes than usual.

This isn’t just a filmmaker trying to get back on track, it’s a filmmaker desperately, nakedly searching for a way to fall back in love with filmmaking itself. A way to prove that it might still love him back. (Kogonada described the project to IndieWire as “A retreat, as well as a pursuit.”)

While the prospect of watching Kogonada do that will naturally be of greater interest to those who have watched him get to this point, this movie’s palpably improvised nature — its stolen shots and recursive shape lend the impression of someone trying to cut their ultra-evocative vacation footage into a coherent narrative — would force anyone to wonder about the meta-textual aspects of its creation. “You feel like your sole purpose in life is something, and it doesn’t choose you back,” L sputters out at one point. “What do you do with that? I had to get away from it all. That’s why I came here. Wandering.”

Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed.

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present.

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals.

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes.

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3503. Netflix's Upcoming Sci-Fi Spinoff Takes Exciting Step Forward With New Update

Netflix is preparing for the arrival of one of its highly anticipated spinoffs.

Netflix's upcoming Manifest spinoff series, Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery, has reached another important milestone as development continues on the science fiction drama. After the original show concluded its run three years ago, the franchise is preparing to introduce an entirely new story within its universe. However, while the plot might be new, the spinoff will maintain its connections to the lore that made its predecessor successful.

Created by Jeff Rake, Manifest originally premiered on NBC in 2018 and followed the passengers of Montego Air Flight 828. Shortly after landing, the characters realized that more than five years had passed despite nothing seeming wrong with their flight. They begin experiencing mysterious events known as Callings, leading them to uncover disturbing secrets about their situation.

Although NBC canceled the series after three seasons, Netflix brought it back for a fourth and final season, which ended in June 2023. The show's popularity eventually led to another installment in the franchise, Arrivals, which Netflix officially announced in August 2026. Now, Rake has revealed that Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery has secured a director for its first episode. The creator announced the news on his Instagram as part of his Showrunner Diaries series, which provides viewers with behind-the-scenes information.

While Rake confirmed that someone has been selected to direct the debut episode, the director's identity has not been disclosed at the time of this article's publication. The update also revealed that everything is progressing very smoothly across several departments. The creator explained that they are beginning to form Arrivals' production team, with several positions already filled.

Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery was first announced by Netflix on August 28, 2026, with the date paying homage to Flight 828. The streaming platform confirmed that the upcoming project would feature new characters and storylines while staying true to the Manifest universe.

The spinoff series won't be a direct continuation of the original show's finale. Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery will explore an entirely different incident within the franchise's world. The story reportedly begins when an unidentified aircraft makes an unexpected crash landing in Denver. The people aboard are unable to remember who they are or why they were on the plane in the first place.

There is no confirmed release date for Netflix's Arrivals: A New Manifest Mystery at the time of this article's publication. However, industry speculation predicts that the series will be released on the streaming platform in 2028.

A supernatural drama series created for NBC, Manifest is an investigation of a fictional flight, Montego Air Flight 828, that went missing for five years after a moment of turbulence in the sky. However, the passengers and crew only felt a moment pass despite the rest of the world assuming they were all gone. The "survivors" now try to reacclimate to society as the world has moved on without them - but voices from beyond seem to beckon them somewhere unknown.

#3502. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying

No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

This grounding process is especially important, and especially challenging, when things that should be on the ground take to the air as a part of Ghidorah’s gravity beam. Inoue did an initial pass of the sound effect for the beam that allows Ghidorah to throw whole houses up in the air high enough for our favorite eternally tormented, former Kamikaze pilot Kôichi Skikishima (Ryûnosuke Kamiki) to fly past them. But it wasn’t quite right.

“So I went back into the Foley studio, and I wanted to capture that feeling of something being lifted and rising. I took this very small speaker, and I placed it right next to a bunch of different objects — a sheet of metal or some wood or a water tank — to capture a sound that almost felt distorted,” Inoue said.

That distortion, bounced off different types of objects, captured the sensation Inoue was after: the sonic equivalent of your stomach lifting into your mouth.

“Oftentimes in sound design, when you layer too many sounds or put too much processing on it, it starts to ruin the original material or the original sound that you’ve captured. So this distortion became a very strong foundation. I didn’t add too much post-processing on it,” Inoue said.

What she did do was hand it over to Takeuchi to create the sense of whole blocks caught up in Ghidorah’s gravity beam and preserve the dialogue and add background dialogue, so that we’re always afraid for the human beings in danger during Ghidorah’s rampages.

When Shikishima first flies through Ghidorah’s gravity beam, the sound team really wanted to lean into the character’s emotional response to something that’s mindbendingly horrible. “I added a Doppler effect — so like when an ambulance or a police car drives by and the sound shifts slightly — [to give] the sensation that you’re passing through,” Takeuchi told IndieWire.

It’s that shifting of sound, more than any one particular sound, that adds a scale to the horror beyond what Shikishima or what we can see. “We wanted to be very mindful of the balance and what it was doing and what it was supposed to do for each scene,” Takeuchi said.

“What we were trying to do is take sounds that you would hear in nature and then design and add to it in almost like an extension type of way, and that’s how we make the Kaiju as well as the gravity beam feel more real,” Inoue added.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3501. Netflix's 6-Episode Western Thriller Masterpiece 'Territory' Is 'Yellowstone' Done Right

Taylor Sheridan’s Yellowstone may know a thing or two about running a ranch empire, but the Duttons aren’t the only family ruling the countryside. All the way in the Australian outback, Netflix’s Territory depicts a different kind of ranch life, where human threats are just as vicious as the unforgiving wild. Instead of the Duttons, there's a different family at the story's heart, one that has passed down their cattle ranch for generations.

While Yellowstone and Territory share similar threads — dealing with grief, greedy corporations, and Indigenous groups — the latter does it better. Territory tells a fleshed-out story of succession without reducing its characters to one-dimensional tropes, while offering thoughtful representation of Aboriginal communities. If anything, Territory manages to outdo Yellowstone at its own game.

Territory follows the fictional Marianne Station in Australia’s Northern Territory, currently helmed by the ruthless, aging patriarch Colin Lawson (Robert Taylor). The series is told through the eyes of Emily Lawson (Anna Torv), who is married to Colin’s eldest son, Graham Lawson (Michael Dorman). However, Colin has long detested Emily, seeing her as a threat because of her background as the daughter of cattle thieves. Like Yellowstone, the series begins with a family death that throws the ranch’s future into question. The sudden death of Daniel Lawson (Jake Ryan) is a blow to Colin, who has always favored his younger son over Graham.

This Netflix series has united two neo-Western giants, and it's about time.

Daniel is supposed to be the inheritor, but his death directly complicates the station’s succession, forcing Colin to choose between the alcoholic Graham and his grandson Marshall (Sam Corlett), who wants nothing to do with the family. Emily believes she’s up to the task, but given her bitter relationship with Colin, convincing the Lawsons to put Marianne under her leadership is easier said than done. With rivals surrounding them and looking to take what they have, the family doesn't have the luxury of time to make that choice.

One of the major flaws with Yellowstone is how Sheridan writes its female characters, typically shaping their personalities in relation to the Dutton men around them. Given her tough upbringing in the Dutton household and fueled by her hatred for her brother Jamie (Wes Bentley), Beth is the de facto “badass” woman. This is portrayed through both her smaller habits, from her cussing to her chain-smoking, and more serious traits, such as her penchant for physical altercations. The same one-dimensional writing applies to Kayce's (Luke Grimes) wife, Monica (Kelsey Asbille), who is primarily defined by the endless trauma caused by her marriage into the Dutton family.

Territory, on the other hand, doesn't box its women into one mold. Instead, it recognizes that women can be many things at once. Emily has all the brains in the world to run Marianne, but she also makes a brash personal decision involving her husband when her heart gets in the way. Her daughter, Susie (Philippa Northeast), is naive enough to waste her university education working at the ranch, but she's also quick to learn the ropes. Meanwhile, Keeley Redford (Tuuli Narkle) serves as a strong-willed community spokesperson who advocates for uplifting the Indigenous community, which continues to lack resources, from proper facilities to job opportunities.

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

For a show that heavily features a fictional Indian reservation (the Broken Rock Reservation), Yellowstone is occasionally guilty of questionable Indigenous representation, something Lily Gladstone herself has publicly criticized. Besides mining Monica for trauma, the show also portrays Indigenous characters as antagonists intent on taking land that “rightfully” belongs to the Duttons. Case in point: Thomas Rainwater (Gil Birmingham). Despite his credentials as a Harvard graduate, former finance worker, and current Chief and Chairman, his fight to reclaim the land is overshadowed by bureaucratic maneuvering and casino politics, ultimately framing him as a greedy chief who takes advantage of the reservation's gambling crisis.

Meanwhile, Territory handles Indigenous representation with greater consideration, thanks to the involvement of Indigenous writers Steven McGregor and Kodie Bedford. Rather than focusing primarily on high-level bureaucracy, Territory gives working-class Aboriginal Australians a central role in its story— particularly through the experiences of Nolan Brannock (Clarence Ryan), a half-white, half-Aboriginal cattle rancher. Caught between two contrasting worlds, Nolan struggles to succeed in the white-dominated cattle industry while remaining loyal to his community. His efforts to create economic opportunities put him at odds with Indigenous elders like Uncle Bryce (Hamilton Morris), who fear financial advancement will come at the cost of exploitation and of Nolan turning his back on his roots in the name of progress.

With all the elements above, Territory has outdone all seasons of Yellowstone in just six episodes. While that makes it all the more disappointing that the Netflix series was abruptly canceled after just one season, it also means that the show is a satisfying binge from start to finish.

#3499. Letterboxd’s Sale to the New York Times: 9 Pros, Cons, and Big Questions from the $330 Million Deal

After several months of business talks and speculation, Letterboxd is about to have new owners. The New York Times is closing in on deal to acquire the film-logging social media platform, which values the company at $330 million. It’s an eye-popping increase from 2023, when the Canadian holding company Tiny bought a majority stake at a $50 million valuation.

Far beyond the film industry, there is a dismal track record and daunting uncertainty when it comes to companies’ ability to maintain their identities after being acquired. Social media reception to the pending New York Times deal generally peaked at resigned relief (“the best case scenario” was a common refrain) while also drawing more cynical, even existential responses about the future of Letterboxd. As the website’s user base holds its breath over the future, these are some pros, cons, and big unknowns to consider about where Letterboxd is going. Related Stories Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

There’s understandably a lot of negative social chatter about the news of Letterboxd’s looming acquisition, but let’s rest assured that it’s at least not a studio taking ownership of the wildly popular cinephile engagement platform. A24, Sony, Netflix, and Skydance were all reported to have registered talks about an acquisition. Whether or not this new iteration of Letterboxd will exist behind a paywall is one matter, but that’s not the worst thing compared to the potential studio-ification (i.e. A24-ification, as they were in talks for the sale) of the brand. Compare it to studios running an exhibition chain — not just Sony purchasing Alamo Drafthouse, but all the way back to the days before the Paramount Decrees, which legislatively blocked studios from having a monopoly on theaters. (Decrees that are no longer in effect.) In that situation, there’s more potential for marketing nepotism and favoritism to titles and properties in-house. A media company taking over Letterboxd should, in theory, prevent the kind of self-interest that threatens independence. —Ryan Lattanzio

A deal would bring two unusually loaded cultural conversations under one roof. The movie-logging platform has helped reshape the world’s repertory film scene — effectively gamifying the enjoyment of archival art — while debates about the Times often wind their way back to the paper’s coverage of Palestine and trans rights. For Letterboxd users who see that coverage as having real consequences for whose lives and experiences are taken seriously by mainstream journalistic institutions, the prospect of the Times owning a community they helped build raises questions of trust. A bigger audience would be a genuine upside, but for some users, who owns the room is an existential issue. —Alison Foreman

While some users might not even know about Letterboxd’s digital magazine, the Journal has been a growing presence on the platform, with a staffed editorial team regularly publishing interviews, retrospective considerations, film festival coverage, and other longform articles. The question remains on how, or if, those writers and editors will be integrated into the New York Times newsroom. A shuttering of the Journal would wreck yet another publication for professional film coverage and freelance opportunities, of which there are fewer and fewer. On the other hand, when the New York Times bought The Athletic in 2022 for a whopping $550 million, the banner initially continued as a semi-independent banner. But a year later, the Times dissolved its existing sports department, laying off or reassigning staff, and positioned The Athletic as a replacement. The New York Times’ culture desk has not been immune to shake-ups over recent years; the potential addition of Letterboxd begs the question of whether further changes are in store. —J. Kim Murphy

As the number of Letterboxd accounts has skyrocketed over the past few years, navigating the platform has become a bumpier experience for users. Pop-up Cloudflare turnstiles reading “Verifying you are human. This may take a few seconds” make frequent interruptions clicking from page to page, while Gremlins-centric error messages signaling server crashes are semi-regular occurrences. The New York Times draws much more web traffic than Letterboxd and such technical hiccups are essentially anomalous. The company certainly has the resources to bolster the strength of Letterboxd’s servers. —JKM

Letterboxd users have historically been an extremely discerning audience, sensitive to changes that might be seen as minute or inconsequential for other websites. A memorable hiccup from recent years came when the platform abruptly removed an option to list out all star-ratings given by the accounts one follows on a single web page. After some backlash from users (like myself) who noticed the feature’s disappearance, Letterboxd was swift in reintegrating the tool. It was a small crisis with a happy ending, but it speaks to how quickly UI changes can dishearten the platform’s users. If the New York Times wants to make even small tweaks to the platform, or heavily integrate it into its digital ecosystem, it will face an audience that’s quick to rally against such changes. —JKM

The New York Times Company is the poster child for brand elasticity in the digital media age. America’s newspaper of record didn’t just adapt to the Internet; it built an empire of games, recipes, and sports that a sizable chunk of the world needs to engage with in a daily basis. But it’s less apparent how Letterboxd fits into the strategy. The social network exists somewhere between an editorial product and a game and doesn’t have a clear comp within the NYT organization. Is the plan to simply move the entire Letterboxd infrastructure behind the NYT paywall, making the $30 monthly subscription tier even more unavoidable for cinephiles? Draw on users’ data to bolster revenue opportunities for streaming promotions and the Times’ product recommendation banner Wirecutter? The answer might be some combination of the above, but the Times is entering uncharted territory. —Christian Zilko

Plenty of filmmakers IndieWire has spoken to are concerned about the widening gap between what defines film criticism and what defines a hot-take social media sound-off, i.e., the “instant reaction.” Reviews on Letterboxd can range from the thoughtful and long-form to the pithy and snarky. As film critic jobs evaporate globally, what happens when you merge Letterboxd closer to the purview of established, institutional film writing, the kind that’s hard, that demands a chunk of your soul? Letterboxd has further democratized criticism, no question, and while many of us argue that we need an elevated discourse, what happens if more people start to think… we don’t? Will the fusion of the Times and Letterboxd stoke that debate, or create harmony? Will this only fuel the growing primacy of influencers over critics and journalists as an authority on a film’s quality? Either way, cantankerous conversation will abound. —RL

It follows then that if enough Letterboxd users distrust the Times, they might log fewer movies, post fewer reviews, or exit the app altogether. From a web-development perspective, the basic mechanics of a movie diary are incredibly easy to replicate. (Hell, AI just cloned Adobe Photoshop.) The hard part is getting the consumers whose aggregate taste is a cultural bellwether to once again show up in the same place. It wouldn’t take a mass exodus for Letterboxd to feel fundamentally different, and if the core group of people who reliably made consumers laugh or put weird repertory picks on your radar stop contributing, there will be fewer reasons to engage. The community could splinter across new competitor sites — which, yes, opens up potential opportunities for aspiring critics to gain exposure and find their followings. But we can’t know if any of that would be as big as the OG Letterboxd. —AF
