#3465. 8 Netflix Romance Shows Where Every Episode Is a Masterpiece

The best romance shows on Netflix understand what fans actually want: the kind of yearning that rewires your brain chemistry and characters who grow into people worthy of the love story they're in. The series on this list deliver that, plus enough swoonworthy scenes to make you pause the episode and stare at the ceiling for a minute.

They know that a good romantic setup means nothing if the show doesn't earn the payoff, and they do the work, episode after episode, building tension and affection until you're mad at yourself for needing sleep instead of pressing play one more time. Whether you're in the mood for Regency-era scandal, a slow-burning British heartbreak, or a teen love story that somehow makes you cry harder than any adult drama, this list has you covered.

Shonda Rhimes and creator Chris Van Dusen took Julia Quinn's beloved novel series and built the most addictive period romance on television around it. Each season of Bridgerton follows a different sibling on the hunt for love in an alternate-history London where the ton is racially integrated, the gowns are absurd (complimentary), and Lady Whistledown (voiced by Julie Andrews) narrates everyone's worst decisions. Season 1 introduced Daphne (Phoebe Dynevor) and the Duke (Regé-Jean Page) in a fake-dating plot so effective it launched a thousand fan edits. Season 2 slowed down for Anthony (Jonathan Bailey) and Kate (Simone Ashley), Season 3 gave the internet's favorite pairing in Penelope (Nicola Coughlan) and Colin (Luke Newton), and Season 4 turned to Benedict (Luke Thompson) and Sophie (Yerin Ha) in a Cinderella retelling that landed in two parts earlier this year.

Four seasons in, with a fifth and sixth already confirmed, Bridgerton has figured out how to reset its love story every year without losing the world it's built around it. The supporting cast rotates in and out with the confidence of a show that knows it has depth on its bench. And the eight-episode season format means nothing overstays its welcome. You'll be fanning yourself before the corsets ever come off in this one.

When the trailer dropped for Nobody Wants This, the internet collectively decided Kristen Bell and Adam Brody had no business being that charming together. Then the show premiered and proved everybody right. Created by Erin Foster and loosely based on her own life, the first season follows Joanne (Bell), an agnostic sex-and-dating podcaster, and Noah (Brody), a newly single rabbi, as they fall for each other and immediately discover that every person in both of their lives has an opinion about their inter-religion romance. The banter is sharp, the chemistry is ridiculous, and Justine Lupe as Joanne's sister Morgan is doing career-best work as the family member who says everything the audience is thinking.

Three seasons in and the show has only gotten more confident in what it does well. Season 3, which dropped in October, pushes Joanne and Noah past the will-they-won't-they and into the thornier territory of actually building a life together, while Morgan's rising media career and the long-simmering tension between her and Sasha finally gets real screen time. The fact that each season has managed to deepen the central relationship without manufacturing drama where none was needed feels pretty special in this day and age.

The Netflix adaptation of David Nicholls' 2009 novel One Day follows Emma Morley (Ambika Mod) and Dexter Mayhew (Leo Woodall) across fourteen years, checking in on the same date every episode. They meet at their Edinburgh graduation in 1988, and from there the show tracks the friendship, the missed timing, the terrible boyfriends, the worse haircuts, and the slow gravitational pull between two people who keep almost getting it right. Mod is phenomenal as Emma, a woman whose intelligence and self-doubt wage a constant war, and Woodall plays Dexter's early-career arrogance with enough buried tenderness that you never fully give up on him.

What makes the fourteen-episode limited series work is the pacing. One day per episode means small moments add up, doing the heavy lifting that a lesser show would try to accomplish through big dramatic speeches. If you haven't watched it yet, go in cold. You might hate us afterward, but then you'll probably watch it again.

Alice Oseman adapted her own graphic novel series for Netflix and somehow created a show that is both completely earnest and totally immune to the cringe that usually comes with that kind of sincerity on television. Heartstopper follows Charlie Spring (Joe Locke), an openly gay student at the fictional Truham Grammar School, and Nick Nelson (Kit Connor), a popular rugby player who starts questioning his sexuality after the two of them become friends. The supporting cast, including Yasmin Finney, William Gao, Corinna Brown, and Kizzy Edgell, gives the show a warmth that extends well beyond its central couple, and Olivia Colman's recurring role as Nick's mum is a casting decision that couldn't be more right.

The show wrapped its main television run in October 2024, and the feature-length film, Heartstopper Forever, landed in July 2026 as a proper send-off. What's remarkable about the series is how it expanded its scope across those three seasons without losing its emotional center. Mental health, identity, family pressure, and the overwhelming terror of being a teenager who feels everything all got serious screen time, but the show never turned into an issues drama. It stayed a love story first, which is why it's on this list.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

The comparisons to Gilmore Girls showed up before the first episode of Ginny & Georgia even aired, and while they aren't entirely wrong, they also sell the show short. Brianne Howey plays Georgia Miller, a thirty-something single mother who moves her two kids to an upscale New England town while outrunning a past that includes enough criminal activity to fill a completely different show. Antonia Gentry is Ginny, her fifteen-year-old daughter, who can sense that her mother's sunny persona is covering something dark and resents being the only one in the family willing to ask questions about it. The dynamic between Howey and Gentry is the engine, but the romantic side plots are just as juicy.

Ginny and Marcus (Felix Mallard) have one of the messier, more honest on-off dynamics on teen TV. It's the kind where you root for them even when they're making each other miserable. Meanwhile, Georgia's relationship with Wellsbury's mayor, Paul Randolph (Scott Porter), is a slow burn weighed down by every secret she's keeping from him. And her will-they-won't-they with Joe (Raymond Ablack) is simmering with pull-your-hair-out-by-the-roots levels of sexual tension.

This one is brand new and already worth your attention. My Brilliant Career, adapted by showrunner Liz Doran from Miles Franklin's 1901 semi-autobiographical novel, premiered on Netflix in August 2026 with six episodes that move through the Australian bush country. Philippa Northeast stars as Sybylla Melvyn, a young woman from a poor rural family who gets shipped off to live with her wealthy grandmother, for a society debut that she has exactly zero interest in. What she wants is to be a writer. What her family wants is a good match. The gap between those two ambitions fuels most of the action.

Christopher Chung and Jake Dunn play the two men, Harry Beecham and Frank Hawden, who complicate Sybylla's plans and the love triangle the show builds is more interesting than the standard-issue version because Sybylla's resistance to romance isn't an act. She flat-out doesn't want what everyone around her says she should, and the show takes that seriously.

Based on Rachel Cohn and David Levithan's novel, this 2020 holiday series from creator Joe Tracz gave Netflix eight episodes of wintery New York City romance that went criminally under-watched. Austin Abrams plays Dash, a cynical teenager who hates Christmas, and Midori Francis is Lily, an optimistic one who leaves a notebook full of dares on the shelves of the Strand Bookstore. They communicate through the notebook before they ever meet face-to-face, as both characters go on scavenger hunts across Manhattan that double as a slow reveal of who they actually are beneath their respective armor.

Netflix canceled Dash & Lily after one season, but the eight-episode run is self-contained enough to work as a complete story. Abrams and Francis play off each other with an easy chemistry, and the supporting cast fills out the world around them with plenty of warmth and humor. Queue it up when you want your romance a bit more seasonal.

Ali Novak's novel started on Wattpad, and My Life with the Walter Boys has spent three seasons turning that scrappy origin story into one of Netflix's most reliable YA franchises. Nikki Rodriguez stars as Jackie Howard, a Manhattan teenager who moves to a Colorado ranch after a family tragedy. She finds herself living with the Walter family and their sprawling, chaotic household full of boys with too many feelings and not enough communication skills.

Noah LaLonde and Ashby Gentry play Cole and Alex Walter, the two brothers who become the points of a love triangle that the show handles with more maturity than you might expect. The Colorado ranch setting gives the show a visual identity that separates it from the crowded field of teen dramas set in anonymous suburbs, and the Walter family's size means there's always a subplot cooking. You'll start watching for the love triangle and realize three episodes in that you're emotionally invested in every single Walter kid.

#3463. 25 Best Seinen Manga Of All Time, Ranked

There's no doubt that shonen series are among the most popular types of anime and manga. Yet, while they can be enjoyed by a broad audience, they are primarily aimed at young males. Fortunately, there is a whole world of options within the seinen category for readers looking for more mature stories. Appealing to a young adult demographic, what is interesting about seinen is that it's not limited to action-driven series, offering a wide variety of genres, ranging from sports and thrillers to battle manga, including many masterpieces that rank among the best in the industry.

Since seinen is aimed at young adults in their late 20s, its works often explore darker themes, more explicit violence, existential questions, and life dramas that a more mature audience can fully appreciate. However, while this category is typically associated with complex, narrative-driven series, it also encompasses slice-of-life stories and other, more niche types of manga that are difficult to classify. This offers seinen readers the chance to delve into stories they might not have initially considered, leading them to discover manga gems that could well become some of their all-time favorite series.

Coolkyousinnjya’s Miss Kobayashi’s Dragon Maid stars Kobayashi, an overworked office worker who gets drunk one night and saves the life of a dragon who had been stabbed with a sword. The dragon, Tohru, is so thankful that she takes on a human form and becomes Kobayashi’s live-in maid, and their developing relationship leads to Kobayashi constantly learning more about Tohru’s world and the complexities of the people who inhabit it.

Not only does the series have surprisingly good fight scenes and worldbuilding, but Miss Kobayashi’s Dragon Maid's character writing always stands out for its stellar development and thoughtful execution, especially when it comes to Kobayashi and Tohru’s relationship. It’s a far more heartwarming story than it appears, and it’s plenty worth reading as a result, even if it does tend to be a little too raunchy.

Aki Hamazi’s Bocchi the Rock! stars Hitori Gotoh, a girl with crippling social anxiety who learned the guitar in a failed attempt at making friends until the day she ran into a girl begging her to be the guitarist for her band, Kessoku Band. Now finally having a proper outlet for her music, Hitori, now nicknamed “Bocchi”, will use her time in Kessoku Band to both make friends and slowly learn to overcome her social anxiety.

Just like the hit anime of the same name, Bocchi the Rock! excels through its thoughtful and often surreal exploration into social anxiety, and the comedic character writing and pleasing artwork to accompany it always works to sell that even further. Anyone who was a fan of the anime will find plenty to love about the manga, as well, especially when it's currently the only way to keep progressing through the story.

In Shinya Umemura, Takumi Fukui, and Azychika's Record of Ragnarok, all the gods in the universe have decided that humanity has become irredeemable and needs to be erased, but the valkyrie Brunhilde offers an alternative. Rather than just erase humanity outright, the 12 strongest gods will fight history's 12 strongest humans in a tournament called Ragnarok, giving humanity a chance to fight for their right to exist and the gods a chance to definitively prove their superiority.

2026 has been an amazing year for manga, and these are the best ongoing titles every manga fan needs to start reading as soon as possible.

Record of Ragnarok is a story that's very much all about fighting and little else, but fortunately, Record of Ragnarok's gorgeous artwork and fight choreography always results in incredible action in every fight, and the few bits of depth the characters are afforded are plenty great to see, as well. There are few manga as good at pulling off pure action as well as Record of Ragnarok, and that's unlikely to ever change.

Fantasy and high-octane action will always attract plenty of attention, but Kenji Inoue and Kimitake Yoshioka's Grand Blue is a welcome change of pace. Grand Blue is a grounded seinen slice-of-life/coming-of-age comedy revolving around college student Iori Kitahara. He's looking forward to starting this new phase in his life, staying in a room above his uncle's diving shop.

Iori tries to steer clear of the antics of the diving club there, who are more interested in partying than actually diving, but eventually gets roped into the group's exploits and learns more about diving through his cousins. It's become a fan favorite when it comes to seinen manga in the slice-of-life genre, with an anime adaptation by studio Zero-G earning a strong reception as well.

Fujisakimori and Bakotsu Tonooka's Rosen Garten Saga takes place in a world where all myths are true, although they often have far more sexual bends to them than their real-life counterparts. When the village of the inexplicably ostracized Lynn is attacked by vandals, Lynn is saved after being possessed by the legendary warrior Siegfried, and while she hates the perverted situations he forces her into, she'll go along with it to try and win the heart of the beautiful warrior Brunhilde.

While Rosen Garten Saga often makes sex, rape, and fetishes integral to its story, not only does it end up looping back around to pure absurdity, but it's paired surprisingly well with Rosen Garten Saga having some of the best artwork and most creative fight choreography of any modern manga. Rosen Garten Saga is one of the best seinen manga around and is great for fans of pure action.

Inio Asano's Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction starts three years after an alien spaceship appeared above Tokyo. The aliens have done nothing in that time, but they've still sparked conflict and discussion around the world as people can't agree on what to do about them. For the most part, though, Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction is unconcerned with all of that and focuses primarily on the daily lives of Kadode, Oran, and their circle of family and friends.

Between its unique character writing and cutting social commentary, a plot that never fails at building tension with every volume, and some of the most gorgeous artwork in any manga, there are no stories with as unique a take on slice-of-life storytelling as Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction. It's not Inio Asano's most famous work, but any fan of his would be remiss to pass up such a clear modern classic.

One of the best fantasy manga of the last decade, Witch Hat Atelier is a prime example of a story that possesses greater depth than it might appear at first glance. The story kicks off when Coco, a young girl fascinated by magic even though it's a practice kept strictly secret from ordinary people, breaks the taboo by witnessing a spell being cast. As the entire course of her life is irrevocably changed, Coco becomes a magic apprentice.

With its highly original approach to magic, taking the time to demonstrate how the mechanics function, and a world rich in lore, Witch Hat Atelier stands out for its complex characters and for being significantly darker than its cast of young girls might suggest. Witch Hat Atelier features stunning artwork and a story that, while sometimes harsh, only gets better as it progresses.

Ryoko Kui’s Delicious in Dungeon opens with Laios' adventure party being wiped out by a dragon and Laios’ sister, Falin, being eaten alive. What’s left of Laios’ party must hurry back through the dungeon to revive Falin, but they lack the funds a party would normally need to do so. Laios’ solution, much to everyone’s chagrin, is for them to eat the monsters they encounter in the dungeon, although for Laios, it’s less a survival tactic and more a dream of his he finally gets to fulfill.

While mostly a comedic take on JRPGs, what truly sells Delicious in Dungeon is its stellar artwork and writing combined with its creative and intricate world building that only gets better as the story progresses. Because of that, Delicious in Dungeon is one of the best takes on classic fantasy in recent years, and anyone looking for something like that won't be disappointed.

Haruko Ichikawa's Land of the Lustrous is a visually beautiful and creative fantasy seinen manga. As eye-catching as Ichikawa's emotionally expressive art style is, the series doesn't slack on depth in the story department, either. The story follows Phos, a member of a humanoid jewel-like species of beings who are deemed weak by their peers in their war against the Lunaris, who want to hunt them down for their value as jewels.

As the story goes on, Phos discovers that their powers come at a brutally steep cost. These revelations gradually unwind in a shocking fashion, and Land of the Lustrous' CG anime adaptation garnered special praise for accomplishing the rare feat of creating exceptional 3D animation that does justice to one of the best seinen manga out there.

Although Chica Umino’s previous work, Honey and Clover, belonged to the josei demographic, the universal appeal of March Comes In Like a Lion makes it easy to see why it was a better fit for a seinen magazine. The series revolves around Rei Kiriyama, a teenage professional shogi player whose life gains color after he meets the Kawamoto sisters.

Seinen anime is a provocative collection of subgenres, often depicting mature or taboo topics, some capable of standing the test of time.

Rather than being pigeonholed as a slice-of-life or sports manga, March Comes In Like a Lion is a story filled with human drama. It goes beyond Rei’s perspective, exploring the inner psychology of its characters, exploring themes like depression, bullying, and family issues, and using visual metaphors drawn from games of shogi or everyday struggles in a brilliant way. Even secondary characters are masterfully developed, making every chapter a delight. This makes March Comes in Like a Lion a story meant to be experienced, so it's no surprise that its two-season adaptation ranks among the highest-rated anime of all time.

#3458. iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

iOS 27.3 beta 1 launched today with a variety of new features, including a big upgrade for one-handed iPhone Duo use thanks to Reachability.

When iPhone Duo reviews first arrived last month, some complained that the extra-wide design of the outer display made it difficult to use one-handed.

At the time, Apple said that it would introduce Reachability via a future software update to help.

Today with iOS 27.3 beta 1, Reachability has officially arrived for iPhone Duo users.

Unlike Reachability on other iPhones, which shifts the screen down vertically, the iPhone Duo version works horizontally.

Once the feature is enabled (Settings ⇾ Accessibility ⇾ Reachability), a short swipe to the side of the screen will shift everything to the left or right, making it easier to reach.

If you’re struggling at all with one-handed iPhone Duo use, iOS 27.3 might make a big difference.

Currently iOS 27.3 is only available in developer beta, but a public beta is expected to launch in the coming days. However, if you’re concerned about bugs or performance issues, we recommend waiting for the launch version. Apple has said that iOS 27.3 will ship to all users next month, with mid-December the most likely window.

Have you tried Reachability on iPhone Duo yet? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3457. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

#3456. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3454. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3453. Prime Video's New Fantasy Series Dangerously Skips The First 3 Chapters Of The Source Material

Prime Video is all set to deliver one of its most ambitious adaptations in the near future. While it is hard not to be hyped about the upcoming adaptation, it is surprisingly taking a major risk. Instead of approaching its source material from the very beginning, the series in question is dangerously skipping 3 major chapters of the original story.

The show, God of War, already seems to have a lot going in its favor. It has Dave Bautista as its lead, Kratos, while other promising actors, like Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Teresa Palmer, and Mandy Patinkin, have also joined its roster. The show is also being created by Ronald D. Moore, who has previously established his creative vision with shows like Battlestar Galactica and Outlander.

Even before its premiere on Prime Video, the God of War live-action series has also been given a two-season order. Interestingly, though, instead of approaching its original game like most other adaptations, the live-action God of War is surprisingly skipping some major early arcs. Will this prove to be a risky creative step for the Prime Video series, or will it actually favor it in the long run?

The early God of War games follow the Greek saga, unfolding Kratos' origins in Sparta. 2005's God of War is all about Kratos' pledge to Ares and his ascension after his first wife Lysandra and daughter Calliope are murdered. In the second and third installment of the games, Kratos walks down a war path as he sets out to seek vengeance against Zeus and the Olympus pantheon.

This eventually culminates in the destruction of Greece.

As confirmed, Prime Video's God of War is skipping the entire Greek Saga, suggesting that the lore from the first three games will not be explicitly spelled out in the live-action adaptation. Instead, the series is setting its eyes on God of War's Norse Saga, which begins with the 2018 game.

In the show's beginning itself, it will be established that Kratos has exiled himself from Ancient Greece before settling down in the Norse realm of Midgard. As the story will progress, Kratos and his son, Atreus, will set out on a quest to spread Kratos' late wife Faye's ashes from the highest peak of the nine realms. This will pave the way for the series to eventually adapt God of War Ragnarök.

For obvious reasons, the Prime Video series will not completely erase the Greek mythology from the games. It will seemingly be explored through flashbacks, highlighting how Kratos' past has shaped him. Still, the show's approach can prove to be risky if the series is not able to establish the contrast between Kratos' violent past in Greece and his attempts to become a better father in the Norse saga.

As risky as the adaptation approach might seem, however, it could prove to be the Prime Video series' greatest strength. While even the Greek saga in the games is brilliantly written, the Norse saga truly puts Kratos' vulnerabilities on full display.

Since a TV adaptation cannot simply jump from one action set piece to another and requires an emotionally dense story, the Norse saga seems to have all the ingredients for a compelling character-driven adaptation.

An actor like Dave Bautista, who has incredible range, also seems perfectly suited for playing a more emotional and rounded Kratos. Even for non-gamers who are not familiar with the source material, the father-son bond from the Norse saga between Kratos and Atreus can offer an instant emotional hook.

Hopefully, the Prime Video adaptation will be as incredible as it already seems to be even though it is making some bold creative choices.

Adapted from the PlayStation video game franchise, God of War is an action-adventure drama series in development under Amazon. The series will center on series protagonist Kratos, but no other information on the series has been divulged.

#3452. 8 Thriller Shows That Are 10/10 Masterpieces, Ranked

Over the years, the thriller genre has provided an admirable number of the greatest TV shows in history. These are series all about sustained suspense, sky-high stakes, and races against time that keep the audience in a constant state of nail-biting anticipation. As such, it should be no surprise that such a naturally engaging genre has provided several TV shows that one can't help but watch from the edge of one's seat.

It's one thing for a show to be great, however, and a whole other thing for it to be so legitimately perfect that it's fully deserving of being called a 10/10. From animated masterpieces like Blue Eye Samurai to live-action classics like Breaking Bad, the most flawless thriller shows in the history of television are proof that even a genre as ambitious as this one is capable of achieving true perfection.

Inspired by the works of Akira Kurosawa and iconic characters like Zatoichi and the Man with No Name, Netflix's Blue Eye Samurai is set in 17th-century Edo-period Japan, following a swordswoman who disguises herself as a man to hunt down the four white men illegally residing in the country. It's one of the best samurai TV shows of all time and proof that animation deserves far more respect among fans of thriller television.

Blending highly cinematic animation with relentless pacing that makes it feel like an unapologetic roller coaster ride, this revenge thriller contains zero filler. It's nothing but non-stop suspense and action, with a perfect balance between story and combat set pieces. Voiced by Maya Erskine, Mizu is an absolutely fascinating protagonist whose journey provides the fuel that makes Blue Eye Samurai such a perfect animated show for adults.

Created by Joe Penhall and executive-produced by Charlize Theron and David Fincher, Netflix's Mindhunter is an adaptation of the true-crime book Mindhunter: Inside the FBI's Elite Serial Crime Unit by John E. Douglas and Mark Olshaker. In it, two FBI agents from the late 1970s revolutionize criminology by interviewing incarcerated killers to understand their psychology and make it easier to catch active murderers.

It's one of the most gripping detective shows of all time, the sort where every episode feels like a puzzle for both the characters and the audience to solve as quickly as possible. Though its cancellation after only two seasons remains one of the most tragic events in the streaming giant's history, Mindhunter nonetheless continues to shine through its masterfully slow-burning narrative, its perfectly written dialogue, and its occasionally horrifying performances.

As if any more proof were needed that Netflix has reigned supreme when it comes to thriller TV shows from the past few years, there's also Narcos, a crime drama chronicling the rise and spread of cocaine drug cartels across the world, as well as the conflicting efforts of law enforcement to meet them head-on. All in all, it's far and away one of the grittiest crime shows of all time and a perfect masterpiece from start to finish.

It's not just Wagner Moura's powerhouse performance as Pablo Escobar, though that has definitely helped to keep the show timeless almost a decade after its conclusion. Rather, it's the way Narcos blends real-world crime history with high-octane fictional elements, constantly pitting its marvelously written antiheroes against its terrifying antagonists. Both as a docudrama and as a visceral action thriller, it works equally well.

Netflix has also produced some exceptional crime thriller miniseries throughout the last few years, which definitely includes the award-winning Adolescence. It follows the harrowing legal fallout for a family of four after the 13-year-old son is arrested for the murder of a female classmate. The series is only four episodes long, but its emotional and thought-provoking effects last for quite a few days after the credits roll on the series finale.

Indeed, it's one of the most perfect Netflix miniseries to date, led by Stephen Graham (who co-created the series with Jack Thorne) at the top of his acting game and a revelatory tour-de-force performance by rising star Owen Cooper. Every episode is shot in a single continuous take, which completely removes the usual comfort of traditional editing and leaves the audience absolutely no room to breathe as they inevitably keep clicking "next episode."

Based on Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata's manga series of the same name, Death Note is one of the most groundbreaking anime shows of the 21st century, certainly one of those essential shows that should be on all anime fans' bucket lists. It follows Light Yagami, a high school genius, who finds a supernatural notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it and decides to use it to purge criminals.

It's one of the most intelligent and perfectly paced cat-and-mouse thrillers that the small screen has ever seen, the ultimate supernatural chess match for people who love anime television — and even for those who have never seen any other anime show before. Perfectly animated and perfectly written from beginning to end, it's such an airtight story that even the most seemingly mundane of actions are imbued with the utmost suspense and tension.

Netflix's first-ever attempt at making a German-language series came in the form of Dark, a science fantasy mystery thriller unlike any other. It's set in a small German town, where the search for a young missing child uncovers hidden secrets and a multi-generational time-travel conspiracy connecting four local families. Everything that ensues makes for what's arguably the greatest time travel and parallel universe sci-fi show the world has ever seen.

At the very least, Dark is one of the best thriller shows since 1990. It was so meticulously planned out from the very beginning that there aren't any plot holes or significant contrivances, a true rarity for a genre like this. An absolute masterclass in tight plotting, foreshadowing, and dealing with themes like determinism and paradoxes, it's such an intricately layered (and intellectually challenging) genre show that it's surprising just how deeply human it feels as well.

Back in April 1986, a catastrophic nuclear accident at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Soviet Ukraine released massive amounts of radiation across Europe. This is the subject of Chernobyl, the kind of show that proves why there's a strong argument to be made in favor of HBO being the undisputed masters of the miniseries format. Seven years after its airing, it's still the second-highest-rated miniseries of all time on IMDb.

Chernobyl pulls absolutely no punches in depicting the harrowing tragedy of not only the actual aftermath of the Chernobyl disaster, but also of all the systemic deceit and bureaucratic cover-ups that surrounded the event before and after it occurred. Thanks to its top-tier performances, elite production values, and some of the most insightful writing that any docudrama from the small screen has ever seen, it's one of those thriller miniseries whose every episode is perfect.

Could there ever be any question? When talking about the greatest crime shows, thriller shows, or drama shows in the history of television, what series could possibly come out on top if not the one that's most often hailed as the greatest TV show of all time? It is, of course, Breaking Bad, one of those drama shows that have aged like fine wine. At the beginning, its ratings were pretty modest, and it nearly faced cancellation. However, after the series became available on Netflix ahead of Season 4's airing, it quickly turned into the hugely bingeable phenomenon that it's still remembered as today.

Breaking Bad is to television what The Godfather is to cinema: A crime drama of such tremendous quality that even those who don't love it understand why it's so hyper-acclaimed. The performances are perfect, the writing is perfect, the visuals are perfect, the pacing is perfect; absolutely everything that makes up Breaking Bad is a masterclass. As far as its thriller elements go, rarely has history seen any TV series this effectively suspenseful or exciting.

#3448. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3444. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3442. Dungeon Crawler Carl Meets Vampire Survivors In 9/10 100-Hour Free RPG

The sheer number of games like Vampire Survivors releasing today is utterly staggering. Its overwhelming visuals, endless barrage of upgrades, and deceptively complex gameplay are understandably enticing, further bolstered by the low price point and spec requirements. It is no wonder that Vampire Survivors and its abundance of pretenders have garnered such critical and commercial acclaim, especially in an era dominated by elevator-pitch concepts and a desire to move away from the relentless onslaught of live service fluff.

If the leagues of other games like Vampire Survivors have not yet proved sufficient, then there is another title worth trying. This massive, 100+ hour RPG takes a lot of the very best aspects of Vampire Survivors, sprinkles a healthy dash of Dungeon Crawler Carl-esque elements, and adds a core multiplayer component to craft a compelling experience that you can play completely for free. The best part is that it's a relatively old title, meaning it's had years of updates, improvements, and new features, all of which are available for you to enjoy right now.

With even Warhammer getting a Survivors-like game, it feels as if every demographic has been catered to. This includes, of course, the Dungeon Crawler Carl fans, those looking for an experience closer to an RPG, or at least one involving dungeon delving and deadly boss battles. Fortunately, the long-running MMO (which predates the wonderful Vampire Survivors), Realm of the Mad God, fits this bill perfectly, offering a chaotic, visually overwhelming, dungeon-based, RPG experience with bullet hell, Survivors-esque gameplay.

Released back in 2012, Realm of the Mad God has proven to be one of the most compelling MMOs on the market; its simplistic visuals and compelling core premise, alongside its huge focus on co-operative play and community, have helped keep its player counts consistently high, as has the steady stream of meaningful updates. Easily ranking among the greatest MMOs ever made, Realm of the Mad God, much like Vampire Survivors, understands how to hook the player and keep them coming back.

Its combination of a roguelike and MMO makes for an utterly unique experience unlike any other. It features permadeath, but it doesn't feel as punishing as one would expect from an MMO; the abundance of loot is ever tantalizing, as are the numerous classes you can choose from, the focus on group activities, and every high-stakes encounter that sees the screen awash with pixelated projectiles cascading wildly. Ostensibly, Realm of the Mad God dared to dream of an MMO Vampire Survivors over a decade before it came out.

Being an MMO that has been around for nearly 15 years, Realm of the Mad God features hundreds of hours of content for players to get stuck into. You can also play it for free fairly reliably; its vast array of microtransactions typically skews toward the realm of cosmetics and convenience. Of course, that doesn't mean you won't encounter some level of grind or frustration, but you're bound to get a rather substantial amount of Vampire Survivors-esque fun out of it long before you hit that point.

Realm of the Mad God is currently only available on PC. You can download it via its official Steam store page.

One has to enjoy MMOs, however, in order to truly get the most out of Realm of the Mad God. While it is certainly playable solo, engaging with its guilds or playing with friends is ultimately the main way of enjoying it. Should you engage with its community and co-operative gameplay, you'll have a great time and find yourself with dozens, if not hundreds, of hours of fun. If you've been looking for a Vampire Survivors-like with a dash of Dungeon Crawler Carl sprinkled in, then you should absolutely give Realm of the Mad God a try.

#3441. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s revamped StandBy to other iPhones

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in December. To learn more about StandBy and how to customize its different faces, follow this link.

#3440. The 10 Scariest Horror Books of All Time, According to Goodreads

You won’t agree with this. The person writing about this doesn’t agree with this. But being scared by something that doesn’t really frighten someone else… it happens. Different works of horror work for different people, and sometimes, the scariest stories don’t exclusively (or even partially) belong to the horror genre, and then there are also great works of horror that aren’t scary (mostly horror-comedy hybrids).

Anyway, a certain number of users have voted on one of many polls on Goodreads, specifically one for the “Scariest Books Ever Written,” and that’s the one drawn from here. The books below got the most votes, and there are a fair few usual suspects, alongside some head-scratching omissions, but again, this is a subjective thing and a limited sample size, so perhaps approach with a saltshaker. Plenty of grains in there, one would assume.

It feels natural for Dracula to show up whenever the topic at hand involves groundbreaking horror books or notably scary novels. It is more or less the vampire story to which all others are compared, because even if Dracula didn’t invent the idea of the vampire, it did a lot to recontextualize and further develop such a monster, all the while proving creepy and clever in ways beyond just being about a monster.

Like, Dracula is also an interesting read thanks to its structure, with it being one of the best-known – and also one of the best – epistolary novels. You'll likely know the basics of the story, or at least some of what to expect, if you’ve seen your fair share of vampire movies or read other vampire books before getting to Dracula, but it’s still a rewarding and maybe even necessary read if you're into horror, and definitely so if you're interested in the history of horror, as a genre.

Peter Straub collaborated with another iconic horror author (he will be mentioned a lot below) on The Talisman and its sequel, Black House. If you like those, or if you just like horror in general, then some of Straub’s solo books are also inevitably going to be worth seeking out, with Ghost Story possibly being the best place to start, since it’s his most iconic/essential book.

You do know what you're in for, with that title and also with Straub’s reputation, but to be a bit more specific, it’s about a writer making startling discoveries about his recently deceased uncle, and he also ends up finding a group of people dangerously obsessed with ghost stories. It’s not really explosive, and maybe parts of Ghost Story also feel somewhat old-fashioned, but it’s still a significant supernatural horror story, and it did at least rattle a fair few people who voted on the Goodreads poll in question.

You could really only say that Lord of the Flies is almost a horror novel, rather than directly one, or at least a survival story that manages to be horrific at times. Still, a book doesn’t have to be full-on horror to be one of the scariest ever written, and Lord of the Flies is certainly unsettling, with some of the scare factor potentially being because people tend to read this when they're young, since it’s often studied at school and all.

The basics: it’s about a group of young boys getting stranded on an island, and things get bad more and more as everything goes on, with groups formed and conflict unfolding. Lord of the Flies does quite a lot with a simple premise, and remains compelling for its commitment to realism, and its ability to be dug into and analyzed if you're into doing that (of course, if you're reading it at school, you'll be made to do that whether you'd like to or not).

Carrie is a good place to start with Stephen King, since it’s definitely one of his slimmest books, and it’s also his first published novel. It’s also not a book that messes around or ever gets the chance to drag, and so it’s an easy read in terms of length and readability, but with the content, things are definitely more upsetting and not really describable as easy or breezy, but for good reason.

It’s about a teenage girl who has a horrible home life and faces bullies during most of the time she spends at school, and so the telekinetic powers she has, that are growing in intensity, threaten to explode and cause destruction should she be pushed too far. And it is more a case of when she’ll be pushed too far, rather than if, owing to the way Carrie is structured. Though fantastical with the telekinetic abilities, Carrie might well be scariest with the more mundane horrors alongside that out-there stuff, owing to the way it unflinchingly explores bullying and abuse among family members.

The Haunting of Hill House is an absolutely essential work of 20th-century horror, and so it feels like it’s earned the right to be considered among the scariest books of all time. Like Ghost Story (obviously), it is technically a ghost story, doing the whole supernatural thing, but it finds interesting ways to play with those potentially familiar genre elements, doing more than just supernatural horror, in the end.

Shirley Jackson understood how to blend a few different kinds of horror together for sure, and The Haunting of Hill House has remained influential as well as timelessly scary (look at the well-received miniseries adaptation that didn’t come out too long ago in the overall scheme of things). The Haunting of Hill House is also pretty lean, at a bit under 250 pages, so it’s not a hard book to get into and appreciate, packing a good many unsettling things into what is ultimately a fairly effortless reading experience.

Even if you're someone who’s not read or watched a ton of horror, you're still likely to have heard of The Exorcist. It’s one of those all-timers within the horror genre, particularly demonic possession and religious horror, whether you're talking about the book or the movie version. The premise is the same either way, because it’s about a young girl who starts showing signs she might be possessed by a demon.

Her mother doesn’t want to entertain that as a possibility at first, but things very slowly get worse, and so eventually, there is indeed an exorcism. But the build-up to that is also quietly unnerving, with more of the outward terror coming toward the end of the whole story. It is extremely well-paced, in any event, and also, come on: it’s The Exorcist. Of course it’s effectively horrifying, and naturally, it well and truly has scared a ton of readers over the years.

From this point on, Stephen King absolutely dominates the Goodreads list being pulled from, so apologies in advance if you're not keen on King. Take it up with the users of Goodreads. So, the first of the top 4 (all King) is Pet Sematary, which might well be the heaviest Stephen King novel, so even if all its attempts at horror fell short, it would still be uncomfortably effective at unnerving owing to how tragic it all is.

Pet Sematary is pretty horrifying in ways both expected and unexpected, and the rawness here makes it easy to appreciate and somewhat difficult to recommend.

The premise here involves a cemetery that seems to bring the dead back to life, but at a cost, because of course there’s always a cost, which is something Stephen King also explored in Needful Things, to some extent, and then went all-out in exploring with Revival, which is easy to recommend to those who liked Pet Sematary. Anyway, Pet Sematary is pretty horrifying in ways both expected and unexpected, and the rawness here makes it easy to appreciate and somewhat difficult to recommend, at least compared to a few of the more broadly entertaining Stephen King horror novels (and the ones that aren’t quite as depressing, maybe).

Compared to what came later, Salem’s Lot was pretty slim and not too out-of-control in terms of how many pages it went on for, but if you want to compare it to what came before, it’s a lot more epic in scope. It’s longer and more ambitious than Carrie, and it marked the first time Stephen King went ahead and did quite a lot to populate a whole town of characters, also doing so effectively in the previously-mentioned Needful Things, and doing mostly effectively in Under the Dome.

Salem’s Lot is about vampires slowly taking over a small town, and there’s mystery and a slow build to the whole thing that might've meant it would've been a spoiler, once upon a time, to mention vampires as being a part of the whole thing, but it’s fairly well-known now that this is King’s vampire book. You can know that and still find a lot to be surprised by here, with the whole novel being continually eerie and entertaining, and that loose/unpredictable nature of the plot also making it quite addictive to churn through rather fast.

The Shining isn't quite as claustrophobic as Misery, which didn’t enter the poll being looked at. Though there is another poll for the “Scariest books of all time,” versus the “Scariest Books Ever Written,” and it was on the former poll. Oh well. The Shining does have a few more characters than Misery central to its narrative, but still not too many central characters, in the overall scheme of things. It’s famously about a struggling writer who becomes a caretaker at a mysterious hotel during its off-season, and he brings his wife and young son along with him.

He’s dealing with personal demons and writer’s block, with a certain psychological unraveling happening, and then all that stuff’s exacerbated by the supernatural horror side of things, too. The blend is done quite effortlessly, and The Shining also manages to be one of King’s most immersive novels, for better or worse (you do come to really know the Overlook Hotel, even if you might not want to understand a place that cursed).

There is a ton of variety to the horror found in IT, with it being about a whole lot more than just one frightening clown, even if everyone does know/remember the frightening clown. The titular villain can shapeshift into forms that it believes will most terrify the people it chooses as victims, and so the clown is just one of its forms, with the other maybe being a little harder to depict visually, but just as terrifying when you're reading IT and have to imagine all the horrible sights and situations for yourself.

But IT is entertaining and there are moments of triumph and catharsis here alongside shocking sequences and some really unpleasant stuff. It plays out across two periods of time, since the central antagonist here re-emerges every 27 years, with the same core group of characters fighting It first as kids, and then later on, as adults. Further, you get a ton of world-building and numerous great characters in IT, so if it’s got the most horror of any Stephen King book, all the while also feeling so central to his body of work, then it feels fair for it to top a poll like the one that’s just been covered.

#3438. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3437. Xcode 27.3 adds GitHub Copilot to its built-in coding assistant

Apple released Xcode 27.3 beta 1 today with multiple new features, chief among them an expansion of its built-in coding assistant to support GitHub Copilot. Here are the details.

Since Xcode 26.3, developers have been able to integrate AI coding agents directly into Xcode, to help with tasks ranging from writing boilerplate code to updating entire projects based on their documentation, file structure, and more.

Apple initially introduced ChatGPT integration in Xcode 26, followed by Anthropic’s Claude. Then, in Xcode 26.3, the company expanded both integrations with agentic coding capabilities through OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Agent.

With Xcode 27, Apple added support for Google Gemini, alongside a redesigned interface, interactive planning, and multi-turn conversations.

Now, with Xcode 27.3, Apple is expanding the list of supported AI coding tools once again, this time adding GitHub Copilot.

The Xcode 27.3 beta 1 release notes include the following under the Coding Intelligence section:

As with the other agentic integrations, this is particularly good news for developers whose companies have standardized on GitHub Copilot, as they can now use their company’s preferred AI coding tool directly within Xcode.

Here are the full release notes for Xcode 27.3 beta 1:

Xcode 27.3 beta includes Swift 6.4 and SDKs for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, tvOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Xcode 27.3 beta supports on-device debugging in iOS 17 and later, tvOS 17 and later, watchOS 10 and later, and visionOS. Xcode 27.3 beta requires a Mac running macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later.

See Xcode Support to learn more about compatible platforms and deployment targets.

Xcode 27.3 is expected to be released in December, alongside macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.
